subtopic: NATO-COMMUNIQUE AND STATEMENT FOLLOWING MINISTERIAL MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the ministers of the 15 countries participating in the meeting have unanimously condemned Soviet military
intervention in the domestic affairs of another country. Moreover, it has been agreed that the resulting situation had brought in a factor of uncertainty as to Soviet future intentions with regard to the security of the west. Consequently, they have reaffirmed their determination to protect the members of the alliance against any military aggression, according to the treaty. They have also stated that any Soviet intervention directly or indirectly affecting the situation in Europe or in the Mediterranean would entail an international crisis with serious consequences. They cannot remain indifferent to any new development likely to jeopardize the security of members of the alliance.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)

The members participating in NATO's integrated defence program agreed that in the circumstances there was a need to reassess their defences, and indicated various measures they were taking to ensure that the security of NATO was being maintained at an adequate level. At the same time they reaffirmed NATO's determination to pursue the long term goal of detente in east-west relations and to exploit all opportunities to make progress in disarmament.
In their statements the Canadian ministers cautioned against the alliance overreacting to Soviet actions in Czechoslovakia which, it had been agreed, were not directed particularly against members of NATO. The Secretary of State for External Affairs suggested that while it was natural in the present circumstances to stress the defensive character of the alliance, it was essential that NATO should seek, and should be seen to be seeking, all reasonable opportunities to resume the dialogue with the Soviet union and thus to promote in due course progress toward the peaceful settlement of the issues facing Europe.
The Minister of National Defence explained that Canada was proceeding with its review of defence policy. Meanwhile, he said, we are maintaining our professional forces in Europe and in Canada at their high level of training, equipment and operational readiness.
2832	COMMONS
Statement Following Ministerial Meeting
Arising out of the decision to close one of the three air bases that we occupy in Germany-Zweibriicken-we had planned to reduce the aircraft of our air division by approximately 20 per cent. However, we felt that until there has been a better opportunity for the Canadian government to assess the aftermath of the Czech crisis, both in the light of this meeting and in the light of our own review of defence policy, it would be prudent to defer a final decision on our part whether the air division should be maintained at its present levels or reduced. This, of course, will not affect the decision to close Zwei-briicken.
The Minister of National Defence underlined the progressive qualitative improvement of our forces in all three environments, regular and reserve, and asserted that Canada continues to believe in collective security.

Mr. Speaker, we have heard with some interest the remarks made by the right hon. gentleman. This adds one more to the very long list of varying statements that have been made in and out of the house, on this continent and on other continents. I think we will have to examine with some care the document the right hon. gentleman has tabled in light of what has been said by the Prime Minister in this house and his other more interesting observations made outside the house. We would also like to examine it in light of what is alleged to have been said by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of National Defence at the meetings in Europe.
I would simply add, Mr. Speaker, that as far as the people of Canada and the hon. members of this house are concerned the matter is in a state of very considerable confusion. I only hope and suggest that what will be done is that which has already been suggested, namely that on the return of the Secretary of State for External Affairs the house leaders will arrange for a day to be set aside so there can be a clear cut debate on this issue, in view of the varying statements that have been made and the facts that have come to light.

subtopic: NATO-COMMUNIQUE AND STATEMENT FOLLOWING MINISTERIAL MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we heard the Prime Minister's statement with a great deal of serious reservation. One of the most regrettable results of the utterly unjustified invasion of Czechoslovakia has been to give an incentive to cold war

DEBATES	November 18, 1968
warriors, who are not without influence in NATO, to demand an even greater reliance than before on obsolete and dangerous military confrontations in Europe. There are some who seize avidly on the opportunity to put pressure on allies to multiply weapons that are already useless and, if used, would produce an unimaginable scale of destruction in Europe.
From the statement it appears that the government to some extent has yielded to this pressure. We are to retain in Europe the 20 per cent of the air division that was supposed to return to Canada. This division is part of a vulnerable, useless and obsolete type of defence and there is no reason, so far as we know, why it should be retained. We are not saying we do not need mobile defences, but this sort of defence would not be of help to Czechoslovakia or any other country.
We also have serious reservations about the extension of vague threats as to what might happen outside NATO if certain events occur in the world. These threats are either meant seriously, in which case they ought to be seriously contained in terms of real commitments, or they are not meant seriously and do not add one iota to the credibility of the commitments which have already been made in NATO.
We believe the Czechoslovak crisis and invasion came about through fear. We most earnestly hope that in the review the government is making in this field it will undertake a radical revision of the commitments we have made in and through NATO. We do not advocate withdrawal from NATO although we do advocate that the entire framework of NATO, based on tactical nuclear weapons, ought to be reconsidered.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by leave of the house I should like to table an additional group of 21 recommendations made by the royal commission on government organization
2833
Cape Breton Development Corporation which have been approved by the cabinet, some in a modified form. The government has now approved 208 of the 294 Glassco recommendations. Twenty-six were rejected as having been overtaken by events or as impracticable. There remains a balance of 60 recommendations on which final decision has not been made, but all are being actively pursued.
At this time I would like to pay tribute to the late J. Grant Glassco who, as the house is aware, died late in September of this year. Mr. Glassco was one of Canada's great citizens. We are indebted to him for his many contributions to the development of this country. One of his greatest contributions was his chairmanship of the royal commission on government organization. He earned high approbation for his leadership of the large research team he assembled, and for his wisdom, experience and the enormous amounts of personal time and energy that he devoted to this tremendous undertaking. That such approbation was justly earned is evidenced by the fact that no other royal commission dealing with so many matters of such complexity has to my knowledge ever achieved an equivalent acceptance of its recommendations. Scholars of the future will surely declare the Glassco Commission one of the most significant milestones in the development of Canadian public administration. I am sure there is complete unanimity in this house when I say that his passing is deeply regretted.

Under the terms of the agreement, a person who has worked in a State with which we have an agreement can apply for U.S. benefit to the office of the Unemployment Insurance Commission serving the area in which he resides. Conversely, a person who has worked in Canada and who is residing in a State with which we have an agreement can claim against his Canadian entitlement through the office of the appropriate agency in that State. The retroactive remuneration regulations authorized by order in council P.C. 1964-1417 of September 10, 1964 provide for retroactive remuneration to former employees who, for reasons beyond their control, leave the public service between the effective date of such increases and the date of their approval. The regulations, therefore, are applicable to former employes who have

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-MOUNTED POLICE PROSECUTIONS INVOLVING INDIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday the hon. member for Skeena asked whether the attention of the government had been drawn to a recent statement by Mr. Allan Bate to the effect that in court cases involving native Indian people the R.C.M.P. take sides against these native people and put them in the position of not being able effectively to obtain justice in the courts. This question was taken as notice by my parliamentary secretary, and I should like to reply to it on behalf of the Solicitor General.
Senior members of the force have been in touch with Mr. Allan Bate in order to obtain some clarification. Mr. Bate states that he did

not say the R.C.M.P. is against the native people. He also states unequivocally that he has the highest regard for the force and for members of the force whom he has encountered in his work over the years as counsel. He did say, however, that from his over-all experience no policeman should be put in the position of acting as investigator, accuser and often adviser to illiterate persons involved in offences, and this is more likely to occur in isolated areas policed by the force. In short, Mr. Bate is against the system and not the police, and has undertaken to explain his views fully in writing to the attorney general of British Columbia.

Supply-Auditor General SUPPLY
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Faulkner in the chair.
50. Salaries and expenses of office, $2,427,400.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a few general comments to make. I do not know whether it is the intention of the minister to make a statement but possibly he may have something to say later. I might indicate to you, Mr. Chairman, and to the members of the committee that it is not our intention to unnecessarily delay consideration of this particular vote nor the vote which will follow because the public acccounts committee is now sitting and the Auditor General is appearing before that committee. There will be, therefore, substantial opportunities in the committee to deal with the Auditor General's position and his functions. However, there are a few comments I should make which may invite a reply from the minister.
Some time ago it was suggested in this house, and also in the public accounts committee, that it may well be suitable for the office of the Auditor General to be the subject of a special act of parliament. At the present time, as members well know, all the legislation that relates to the Auditor General is in the Financial Administration Act or in special acts of parliament which call upon the Auditor General to perform the task of auditing the accounts of the corporations which are involved. It was proposed in the public accounts committee, and my recollection is a draft act was submitted to the committee and was the subject of some discussion, that having in mind the independent nature of this officer appointed by the government but reporting to parliament, a special act might well be considered. This bill could be brought before the house at a suitable opportunity, and I should like to have some comments on that suggestion.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Again, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I think the house should have some better way than it now has of dealing with the recommendations of the Auditor General. At present they are put before the public accounts committee, subsequently made the subject of discussion in that committee and then dealt with further in the form of recommendations made in the report of the committee which then comes into the house but upon which no further action is taken. I think it is in the interests not only of the government and the

house but of proper administrative efficiency that some means be devised whereby the recommendations of the committee be made the subject of debate in this house. I am not suggesting that there should be a long debate. I am not suggesting for a minute that the government must accept the recommendations of the committee.
It is well known, Mr. Chairman, that following the lead taken by the right hon. member for Prince Albert when he was prime minister the public accounts committee was given a new impetus, a new life. The chairman of that committee at the time was a member of the opposition party and had a very successful and distinguished career as chairman. Since that time this committee has had the opportunity to function in a non-partisan way more than any other committee of the house.
When this committee has considered in detail the recommendations and proposals made by the Auditor General, has considered his report and come to a determination, I think it is quite improper for no action to be taken on the committee's report. It has been my experience-and I am sure all other members who have served on the committee would agree with me-that to a very large extent the recommendations of this committee are almost always unanimous. In that way it is as non-partisan a committee as can be found. Its recommendations are objective and are directed toward securing a better and more efficient administration of government departments.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, it is surely only fair and proper that some means be found, within reasonable limits, to debate in this house the recommendations of the committee when it reports to the house. One need only examine the last report of the Auditor General to discover that a very large number of the recommendations of the public accounts committee have not been dealt with, have not been considered, and the government has not come to a point of view about them or indicated whether it is for or against them. This certainly does not result in expeditious and effective government operation. I therefore suggest that some consideration be given to this point.
I realize, Mr. Chairman, that I can be told by the minister-and he will be quite right to tell me-that this is a matter for the committee. Nevertheless, I think it has been understood in the past that the report made by the committee withers on the vine and nothing
November 18, 1968

happens. In Australia, they have devised a far better and more efficient way to deal with this problem. The public accounts committee operates under an act of parliament. Its functions are set out by statute. Its appointment is arranged by statute. In the pursuit of its duties it publishes, at frequent intervals throughout the year, a document that sets out the recommendations of the committee side by side with what action, if any, has been taken by the government to implement them. This means that there is available to members of the public, to the government's officers and to members of the Australian House of Representatives at all times a clearcut and balanced interpretation of what the recommendations have been and what the government is doing about them.
I do not know whether this would be the answer to our problem, but I suggest that if there is to be any effective and meaningful role played by the Auditor General some better ways must be found to ensure that when a committee of the house, after serious and lengthy consideration, has made recommendations, those recommendations are the subject of debate in the house and, if necessary, of division in the house. After all, the government does not need to accept the recommendations. If it does not accept them the government should be prepared to come into the house and say why. If in the view of the opposition the matter is important enough to be the subject of a vote, then the house can decide by dividing on the issue.
The final point that I would make is this. On a number of occasions it has been suggested by the public accounts committee that the Auditor General should be joint auditor not only of government departments, crown corporations and other emanations in respect of which he is now authorized to conduct an audit but also joint auditor of all crown corporations. I draw to the attention of this committee a recent experience of this need in connection with one crown corporation, the Company of Young Canadians. I am not going into this question because it is now before a committee of the house, but I suggest through you, Mr. Chairman, to the members of this committee that if a joint audit had been done by the Auditor General and the private auditor, the recent experience might never have occurred.
Not only that, Mr. Chairman, but in circumstances where a change in the appointment of the private auditor is made, which does happen from time to time, I think the continuity that would be provided by the
Supply-Auditor General Auditor General appearing as joint auditor, with his experience and knowledge of the affairs of crown corporations, would be most invaluable. I should like to see the government give consideration to this recommendation. It is not a new one to me; it is a recommendation that has been made on a number of occasions in the public accounts committee.
These are the few suggestions that I make, Mr. Chairman. I do not know whether the minister would care to reply to them. I do know that other recommendations will be coming out of the public accounts committee. I assumed that the estimates of the Auditor General will be coming back to this house some time in the new year in a new form, and consequently as far as we are concerned we do not propose to pursue this matter. We say this without prejudice to our belief that there can be a better and more effective way found to deal with the functions of the Auditor General, but we are not prepared to hold up the estimates at this time. I do not want to inhibit the rights of other members, of course, but we feel that if this item and the other one can in due course carry we might well get into other legislative business later this day so as to try to help the government in its difficulties. However, these difficulties are of its own creation in that it has tried to get through the house the legislative diet that it has set for itself.

Mr. Chairman, I just wanted to state that this year I was named to the public accounts committee and was really quite shocked to find that a number of the situations referred to by the hon. member for Peace River existed. First of all we had a report from the Auditor General indicating the status of the recommendations that have been made by the public accounts committee from time to time in the past. Some 55 recommendations had been made by the public accounts committee, on 20 of which no action had yet been taken.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
There were 16 other recommendations where the executive had indicated disagreement. These matters had been considered and there was disagreement with respect to them. I would judge such decisions on their merits. In 13 instances it was indicated that slow progress was being made. In certain discussions there appears to have been sensitivity on the part of some government members on the committee to the use of the word "slow".
November 18, 1968

Supply-Auditor General The Auditor General used the word "slow" advisedly. Two of the recommendations have been implemented and another two are soon to be implemented. In one case the action taken has not been satisfactory and in another case a recommendation was withdrawn by the public accounts committee.
It can be seen that originally there were 55 recommendations and one was withdrawn by the committee, leaving 54. Of that number only four at this time can be said to have had adequate consideration and treatment. I submit that this is not a desirable state of affairs. It is not adequate and the minister and the government ought to attend to it immediately, particularly since the Treasury Board now fulfils certain functions with reference to items coming under the purview of the public accounts committee.
In the past there have been recommendations with respect to having an Auditor General's act. I understand that an act has been drafted and is ready for submission. I think it can be proceeded with. Could the minister say what action the government is going to take on this matter? Is it intended to bring forward the bill, and how soon? It seems to me that in this area the work of the Auditor General could do much to improve the operations of government as such. He could ensure that the government does a good job and could demonstrate through this act that the government can do as good a job for our society as any other segment of our economy. There is no reason why government cannot be operated as efficiently and effectively as any other part of our society.
The matters raised by the Auditor General need to be studied, and if we had an opportunity more than once a year to study many of the matters which are raised the public would have a good deal more faith in government as such. Bringing in the act would, I think, be in the the best interests of Canada and in the best interests of the state of affairs we wish to achieve in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I wish briefly to reply to some remarks made by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat. The house leader for Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition said that the public accounts committee had not operated generally in a partisan way, nor had its reports been used in a partisan way. The hon. member who has just resumed his seat has used the report of the present committee in a partisan way. I say this because I was a member of that committee

and was present when it brought down its report.
The hon. member tried to say that only four of the 55 recommendations have been subject to government action. I dispute that contention strongly. His interpretation of how the government has acted is partisan. The government has looked at many of the recommendations in the Auditor General's report and has decided it does not agree with those recommendations. That, I submit, is action.
With respect to those recommendations the Auditor General classified with the words "slow progress being made", may I point out that one of those items is with respect to the deficit on second class mail. Even though the government has introduced a bill in this house the Auditor General has still described the action taken as "slow progress being made". I submit that if committee members wish to refer to certain of these items they ought to point out merely that progress is being made. They ought to leave out the adjective "slow", especially when that adjective applies to second class postal rates. The bill has already been passed; yet the Auditor General says the government is making slow progress.
I submit that the point of view of the hon. member of the N.D.P. is completely wrong and his remarks are misleading. He is using the recommendations of the committee in a most partisan way, and I regret that.
May I ask the minister a question. The Auditor General at the first meeting of the public accounts committee said that certain members of his staff worked for the United Nations and its related agencies. He also said they received remuneration for this work. Can the minister say what this remuneration is? In the estimates certain revenue with respect to 1967-68 is indicated as applying to 1966-67. Does that revenue have reference to these international agencies or does it have some other significance? How much revenue is received by the Auditor General and his staff for work that is done for the United Nations and its related agencies?

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to have this opportunity to make a brief statement on the role and functions of the Treasury Board as a prelude to having its estimates considered in this committee.
I feel that the board's purpose and responsibilities and its influence on policy and the allocation of government resources are not as fully understood as those of other government departments. And yet the Treasury Board has been a vital and essential part of our structure of government since confederation, and its role as a central control agency of financial matters and as a policy co-ordinator has steadily grown in important over the years.
The board is a committee of the Privy Council established by statute, having certain delegated executive powers and responsibilities as outlined in the amendments to the Financial Administration Act of 1966. The need for such a federal body to act as coordinator and overseer of the financial affairs of government departments was recognized immediately at the beginning of confederation. It was first created by order in council of July 2, 1867. Two years later, however, with the passing of the Department of Finance Act of 1869 it was made a statutory committee of the Privy Council.
An important stage in the evolution of Treasury Board functions came as a result of the findings of the Royal Commission on Government Organization or the Glassco commission, as it became known. At this point I

would like to repeat the tribute I paid earlier today to the late J. Grant Glassco, who made such a significant contribution to improved public administration. The commission felt that the needs of effective management fell into two general categories:	first, those
associated with the administration of departmental operations, and, second, those involved in the central direction and coordinations of government activities as a whole.
With respect to the central direction and coordination of government activity, the commission pointed out that the policies and programs of each department and agency must be balanced against and harmonized with those of other departments and agencies and that they must justify themselves in terms of their contribution to the general interests of the Canadian people. Thus the authority of each department must be subject to the overriding needs of the government for the general interests of Canadians.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The conclusions and recommendations of the Glassco commission were embodied in the Government Organization Act of 1966. The Treasury Board was established as a separate department of government under its own minister, the President of the Treasury Board.
The Financial Administration Act was also amended and it is from this revised act that the board now derives its current powers and responsibilities. These include financial management, expenditures control and general administrative and personnel policy in the public service.
The effect of the amended act was to establish the Treasury Board even more clearly than before as the agency of government chiefly responsible for formulating central management policy including the financial management functions of short and long range expenditure forecasting, program analysis, estimates preparation, supervision and control of expenditures, leases, contracts, and financial commitments.
Also for the first time responsibility for providing leadership and stimulus to improve management performance in the government service was explicitly vested in the board. However, possibly the most important widening in the duties and responsibilities of the board was in the field of personnel management. In part, as a result of being designated as the principal agent of the government in collective bargaining the board had assigned
November 18, 1968

to it, in addition to its previous duties relating to organization and establishment control, exclusive responsibility for classification, rates of pay and conditions of work, and for determining generally the policy governing personnel management in the public service.
At this point I would like to speak briefly on collective bargaining in the public service. This is a most important subject and I thought that hon. members would be interested in having a report on results to date.
In August, 1963, the government appointed the preparatory committee on collective bargaining in the public service. This committee was established to make preparations for the introduction of collective bargaining and arbitration in the public service, as well as to examine the need for reforms in the systems of classification and pay applying to public servants and prevailing rate employees. It was directed to consult with employee organizations and to make recommendations to the cabinet. The findings of this committee were presented to the government on July 2, 1965. The result of these efforts, the Public Service Staff Relations Act, received royal assent on February 23, 1967.
The legislation contains most of the conventional elements common to all labour relations statutes in Canada: the tripartite labour relations board, freedom of association, unfair labour practices, appropriate bargaining units, the principle of majority support, exclusive bargaining agents, and compulsory collective bargaining.
These are the more familiar elements. The act, however, contains a number of rather unique provisions which in a sense reflect the particular requirements of a national public service. One of the more unique features relates to dispute settlement. Unlike most labour relations statutes the Public Service Staff Relations Act provides two separate and distinct processes for the resolution of disputes arising out of the negotiation of collective agreements.
Disputed matters may be referred to binding arbitration by the Public Service Arbitration Tribunal established under the legislation, or they may be referred to an ad hoc conciliation board, constituted in the familiar fashion, for report and recommendations. The bargaining agent in effect has an option. The legislation, while conferring the right to strike in certain circumstances, contains provisions which are designed to protect the public against the disruption through strike
Supply-Treasury Board action of those services which infringe directly on its safety and security.
The extension of collective bargaining rights to professionals departs from existing practice under most labour relations statutes. Another significant departure is the fact that supervisory employees under this legislation have also been granted bargaining rights. The provisions of the legislation in this regard reflect the fact that supervisory and professional employees in the public service have been members of employee organizations for many years and have traditionally been represented by such organization in discussions with the government relating to their terms and conditions of employment. Managers, of course, are excluded.
The legislation places certain restrictions on the subject matter of collective agreements. No collective agreement, for example, may include any provision that would require legislative action by parliament except for the purpose of appropriating moneys required for its implementation.
The rationale for these restrictions is that employees in the public service have long enjoyed certain benefits by parliamentary enactment, for example, pension benefits under the Public Service Superannuation Act and the principle of merit in appointment by virtue of successive civil service acts. By adopting these provisions parliament decided in effect that the rights to which employees were entitled in these areas should continue to be guaranteed by statute rather than by provisions of a collective agreement.
These limitations also apply in the case of arbitral awards rendered by the Public Service Arbitration Tribunal and reports and recommendations of the conciliation board. No arbitral award and no conciliation board report may therefore contain provisions requiring the enactment or amendment of legislation.
I believe that hon. members will be interested in hearing the results to date of operating under this legislation. Bargaining units have been determined and bargaining agents certified for the great majority of employees eligible for collective bargaining under the legislation. As of this date some 61 units have been determined; 22 in the operational category, nine in the technical category, 19 in the professional and scientific category, six in the administrative and foreign service category, and five in the administrative support category. These units embrace

November 18, 1968
Supply-Treasury Board approximately 175,000 employees, or somewhat more than 80 per cent of the total number of employees eligible for bargaining under the system.
As of today the first 19 agreements entered into under the legislation have received formal ratification. These agreements cover supervisory and non-supervisory employees in the following occupational groups: correctional, fire fighters, general labour and trades, hospital services, lightkeepers and stationary plant operations. They also include agreements entered into with respect to printing trades employees, dockyard employees at Halifax and Esquimalt, letter carriers, mail clerks, postmasters and assistants in the Post Office Department, air traffic controllers, and veterinarians. The number of employees covered by collective agreements at the present time is approximately 75,000.
I would now like to spend a little time discussing our financial administration system and the role and functions of Treasury Board within it.
The basic fundamental principles of this system are that no tax shall be imposed and no money spent without the authority of parliament and that expenditures shall be made only for the purposes authorized by parliament. Along with parliament, cabinet is, however, also an integral part of the functional decision-making process in that it determines the general magnitude of expenditures when it establishes policy in the various fields of government activity. While in practice ministers exercise their collective responsibility for policy in cabinet, most of the detailed supervision and co-ordination of expenditures is delegated to the Treasury Board. It has the important function of rationalizing the requirements of all departments and fitting them into the budgetary picture as a whole.
The administrative procedure which makes this process operative takes the form of two major budgetary submissions by the various departments each year. In May departments prepare and submit to Treasury Board forecasts of activities and expenditures for the next five year period. The Treasury Board analyses these proposals with the objective of the exercise being to allocate available resources among competing requirements of all departments.
On the basis of its analysis the Treasury Board then proposes to the government specific financial targets for each department for

the next fiscal year. After departmental targets have been approved by the government and communicated to each department, work begins on the other annual submission, the main estimates for the next fiscal year. These detailed estimates will, in many cases, differ from the material submitted at the time of the program review to the extent that expenditure cuts have been made in the original proposals and departments have to re-allocate resources among their proposed programs. Treasury Board also reviews and analyses this submission. When the board is satisfied with the estimates, they are submitted to the cabinet for consideration. Once approved by cabinet they are recommended to the Governor General and then laid before the House of Commons.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Today government is big business in every sense-in terms of employees, expenditures and the variety and complexity of its activities. It therefore demands from its central financial control and management agency more than administrative clearance of appropriations and expenditures and a routine scrutiny of management functions in the public service. Modem government requires from such an agency meaningful assessments of new and existing programs in terms of objectives and results and complete and understandable data on such programs so that the government is in the best possible position to make policy decisions.
The Treasury Board is, therefore, constantly striving to improve its performance as a central control agency through the introduction of modern management techniques. For example, the Treasury Board has developed and is now implementing a programming, planning, budgeting approach to resource allocation in the federal government. Program budgeting is concerned with the presentation of expenditure proposals in a way that will enable effective decisions to be made on the allocation of resources. The program budgeting system differs greatly from traditional forms of government budgeting in its concentration on the results and benefits as opposed to just a consideration of the resources required. In this regard, program budgeting should also assist hon. members in their scrutiny of government expenditure proposals. I hope to be given an opportunity at a later date to make a fuller statement on this important subject to the public accounts committee.

It can be said that the Treasury Board acts as the employer, manager and innovator in an administrative sense for the government. These are not easy roles, and we are constantly striving to develop new ways to improve our performance and thereby increase the over-all effectiveness of government operations generally.

Helpful though it was at the time of its passage, the Pension Adjustment Act of 1959 no longer meets the minimum justifiable requirement in the case of those former employees who retired prior to January 1, 1953; and it makes no provision whatever for employees who have retired since that date.

Now, Mr. Chairman, I am absolutely certain that I am betraying no secret when I say that the hon. member for Ottawa East, who was chairman of that committee, believed just as completely as I believed that we were dealing with a government which was acting in good faith, and that that report, having been agreed to unanimously by all parties, would receive favourable consideration by the government in that session which began in the afternoon of May 8, 1967.
One of the things that has puzzled me in the years I have been around parliament, and I know the things one can do and the things one cannot do, is what to do with some of the things that are told to us personally by some of these people. Let me put it this way. The present Minister of Finance, who was then president of the treasury board, and the former prime minister Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, both know what they told me in the months of May and June, 1967, about this legislation. They both know the dates they gave me as to when it would be brought into the house and passed. They both will remember how firm were their assurances. Of course, their problem was to get around the then minister of finance. Nevertheless, their statements to me were as firm as they could be; something was going to be done along the lines of this unanimous report.
May went by, June went by, and still nothing was done. It was not that the government of that day was not reminded of this situation. It was reminded by me as well as by other members, sometimes three or four times a week. We were told to wait, it will be done later. Then July 7 came along and there was a desire to adjourn for a summer recess. I took a rather strong stand. However, I was assured by ministers out in the hall and by backbenchers on the government side, that when we came back in the

The discussion of this subject goes on and on because the government has led us down the garden path. The government let us have a committee, let us make recommendations, gave us this promise, but still all we get is, no. The other day the hon. member for South Western Nova, who represents a constituency of particular interest to me because my ancestral home is in that constituency, tried in a very direct way to get the minister to suggest that there would be some good news before Christmas. The Minister of Finance gave the answer, no. I thought I head some shouts of "Shame" and "Scrooge" on that occasion, but they do not seem to appear on the pages of Hansard.
I submit that the way the government has played with the hopes of these citizens, these former employees, is a sorry story. How many are there? Not enough, of course, to influence an election; they are not concentrated enough to do that. If you add together the

number of retired civil servants and their widows, the retired personnel of the R.C.M.P. and their widows and the retired members of the armed forces who would come under this kind of pension, you may get up to around 60,000 or 75,000 people. They are scattered all over the country, in fact scattered all over the world. The fact is that they are former employees of the government. I submit we have a responsibility to them to be a good employer.
I know the various arguments that are used, even though they are not trotted out in public, against dealing with this matter. I know the main fear is that if the government moves in this field a precedent will be set that will annoy private business in some areas. May I tell the President of the Treasury Board that private business is beginning to deal with the matter. In the years I have been arguing for the government to act, a number of private companies have approved pension plans in which there are escalator clauses so that pensions go up after people retire. We have accepted the principle, at least very slightly, in the Canada Pension Plan and in the Old Age Security Act. There we have a 2 per cent limit, and it does take quite a long while for it to amount to anything and it never catches up with the rise in the cost of living.

In addition to all these factors of right and justice that I think are on the side of these people about whom I am speaking, I should like to say to this minister and to this government that I think this is one of the most serious issues facing us in the whole pension field. It used to be that not many people were on pension and not many people lived for very long after retirement. Thanks to medical science, longevity has increased. Thanks to all these transplanted hearts and everything else, a lot more people continue to live on pension, and as time passes more will do so, for 15, 20, 25 or 30 years.
Imagine anybody in any other sector of the economy being asked to live on the same level of income for a period of 30 years, Mr. Chairman, or for even for half that period! We have to face the fact that our pension program, if people are going to survive and our pensions not be placed in serious jeopardy, must have adequate escalation provisions. I suggest that the place to begin is right here with these our own employees, our retired federal civil servants.

Some bodies, notably the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada and others who have joined with them, have suggested that a look be taken at the rate of interest that the government pays on this money. The rate, Mr. Chairman, is 4 per cent. Where can the government get money today at 4 per cent? It pays 6.75 per cent on money that is invested in Canada Savings Bonds; yet these people are asked to settle for a rate of 4 per cent. The Professional Institute has suggested that maybe it would not be out of line to raise this figure to 5 per cent.

Mr. Chairman, I fully agree with the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), that the retired public servants receive too small a pension, as recognized by the parliamentary committee which looked into the situation. To my mind, the government should have reached a decision last year, or even earlier, with regard to the public service.
The member for Winnipeg North Centre said that they do not live very long after

retiring. Small wonder, with the small pensions they receive, they cannot live very long. That is why we agree with the member when he asks for an increase in those pensions.
We know, for instance, that the pensioners outside Canada who receive an old age pension or allowance, in China, in India, or in Europe, have a cost of living bonus in addition to their pension or allowance, although the cost of living is not as high in those countries as it is here; yet they receive the same pension as retired Canadians.
Taking into account the high cost of living here and the low pension, it is clear-the minister must realize this-that those people cannot survive. The minister and the government may say that this is a financial question, that they do not have the money required. It is always the same story, the same reason: there is no money.
Along the same line of thought, when we ask, for instance, a 7 per cent bonus for bilingual employees of the Canadian parliament, we are told that the decision is incumbent on the Speaker, the Treasury Board, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), and nothing is done.
Are the employees of the House of Commons considered as extraterritorial employees, external employees, employees of the administration of Canada? A bonus of 7 per cent is paid to bilingual public servants in various Canadian departments; but with regard to the House of Commons, they are no longer federal employees, it seems, because they do not get that 7 per cent bonus which is paid to bilingual civil servants under the law.
We have guides at the main entrance and on every floor of the main parliament buildings. We have secretaries, pages, a whole array of house employees to whom the 7 per cent bonus is denied. Why? Because, we are told, there is no money. As the Treasury Board is the one to decide whether or not additional amounts are to be paid to help various groups of society or employees-and with greater reason federal employees-I say that the Treasury Board is responsible for such a situation. For instance, useful works are refused or delayed, because there is no money while useless works are willingly carried out in many fields and they find the required money.
Parliament is asked to place restrictions on credit but have the Treasury Board and its president considered the fact that this year, the government will pay, in interests only, $1.5 billion on the national debt, namely an

Mr. Chairman, we would then be led to believe that there is some political partisanship, even if the minister maintains the contrary, within Treasury Board. We are somewhat sceptical, especially when we are told that Treasury Board acts in the best interests of the Canadian people. The function of the board is to control expenses, according to our fiscal system. When taxes have been collected, it decides if such or such a department may obtain or spend such or such an amount. It makes slight increases in a certain area and slight reductions elsewhere. We are fumbling with that system. Why? Because the government which is responsible for that situation wants to stick to it. In my opinion, the so-called sovereign government is a slavish government which refuses to take decisions without the authorization of the financial system. In addition, the execution of works is delayed. While 300,000 or 400,000 Canadians are unemployed and ready to work, the government chooses to pay them unemployment insurance benefits rather than give them work to create something in our country.
This is the procedure which has been chosen. Who is controlling that system? Some experts and economists. I do not know what kind of economists or experts advise the government but, in any case, we are subjected to a strange system which enables a few financiers to grow richer, while the majority of small taxpayers are getting poorer. That is exactly our situation at the present time.
Expenditures should be controlled instead of adjusting the financial system or our opportunities of developing the country. Attempts are being made to adjust the development of the country to the requirements of a financial system which is totally obsolete. In fact, this is the only thing they do not want to reform.
We hear every minister speaks about reform, in the field of education, farming, labour conditions, public service, reform in that field and in this field, however when it comes to the solution which would reform the financial system, it must be left alone. We must stop there because we do not even have the right to argue.
The Prime Minister of a sovereign country like Canada says: We have only the money that the people are willing to let us administer.
Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the easiest thing to do in Canada is to regulate credit and to put it at the disposal of the Treasury Board.

Making cement, bricks, lumber to create or build something, that is difficult, that takes a lot of hard work. Building a road, a bridge or a school, enlarging a hospital, that is difficult. But the matter of credit, that is easy. With pen and ink to write the figures according to the possibilities to build things in Canada, that is financial stability.
The Treasury Board is caught in a system which sees nothing else but the possibility of the government to levy and administer taxes, to distribute what they yield to the public and the various departments after paying the administration costs. This is exactly the situation with which we are confronted and the honourable ministers know the problem. The ministers and the President of the Treasury Board are perfectly aware of the situation. They know that our natural resources are still at the development stage, in fact some have never been tapped. Universities prepare technicians because we need technicians, engineers and so on. Once they have left university, these boys who could create something, work in assembly plants in Montreal. Engineers who graduated in May or June last year, earn $5,500 to $5,700 a year on car assembly lines in St. Therese de Blainville. Then we get upset, we get excited, and we ask ourselves: How is it that students protest and rebel against the present state of affairs? Sunday afternoon, I watched Father Pierre on television in Montreal. It was incredible to hear him giving the reasons why youngsters today are revolting against the order of things.
People talk about peace, just society, justice and stability. True, but what kind of peace? The peace of those who are considered as the establishment and whom are not to be disturbed, because they feel comfortable. It is in such a peace that we are working today.
Youngsters cannot see how they will be able to identify themselves within such a society when they get out of university. This is the opposite of what we used to see 20 years ago when a student leaving university could find a job immediately. Today, it is not the same thing. Public works are no longer undertaken for financial reasons; rather, the young are left in a state of anxiety about the next day, they cannot even merge into society. Then, they will be accused of being rebels or revolutionaries.

However, a simple mathematical operation shows us that if we produce $70 billion in products and services, and if our production increases by 6 percent during the course of the year, the increase will be $4,200 million. If our national income reaches $50 billion and if we cannot increase it above our productivity, i.e. 6 percent, the increase has to be $3 billion. Then, let us allow salary increases of $3 billion, so that the population will buy the production increase of $4,200 million; there will still remain a gap of $1,200 million. The government does not understand that. There still are ministers who do not know that 2 and 2 make 4; they want it to make 5. From a mathematical point of view, they are way off.
Others cry out: Fine, but where are the $20 billion? In towns and cities, store shelves overflow with products to the extent where no one knows what to do with the goods. There is a lack of purchasing power, and instead of increasing it, the government levies taxes, claiming that by so doing it checks inflation.

Increase the pensions of the former public servants; with that we agree, no one fears inflation. But there would be danger of inflation if a dividend were distributed to the whole population.
Mr. Chairman, in closing my remarks, I would say this to the minister: if he has no solution to suggest, it is time for him to come with me on television, every week, to teach Social Credit to the people, so that we can be rid of an irresponsible government and appoint in its stead one capable of assuming its responsibilities.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, I know that before six o'clock I can raise and expatiate on the matters that I want to draw to the attention of the President of the Treasury Board. I also know it is a damn sight more important for the President of the Treasury Board to be speaking to his friend across the aisle, but I would like to hold the floor without speaking and without losing any time until the President of the Treasury Board is prepared to listen to what a member on this side of the house wants to draw to his attention. I have now got his attention. I think, Mr. Chairman, it is very important that when members on this side of the house raise matters they should have the attention of the minister in charge.

Through you, Mr. Chairman, I want to draw what I consider a most serious matter to the attention of the minister. I know I do not have authority to speak on behalf of the some 160,000 employees of the federal government, but I do think I have the right to draw to the attention of the President of the Treasury Board some aspects of a matter concerning some 160,000 employees of whom 102,000 are in the armed forces. In the last year or two changes have been made in negotiation
November 18, 1968

procedures and regulations and in respect of authority when dealing with management on matters affecting wages and conditions of employment of those within the civil service. However, in the legislation governing negotiations between the government and its employees there is a section which says that once a contract between the government and its employees is signed or an agreement is reached the government of Canada does not have to accede to it for 60 days but at the end of the 60 days must pay the increase and any retroactive payments.
It is a fact that in the last few weeks a number of contracts have been signed. I only know through reading the press how this affects the armed service personnel. However, if my analysis is correct, and I think it is, as a result of arrangements made in respect of armed service personnel and the other con-tractal agreements made by the government with its civil service employees there are now over 150,000 persons who are entitled to increases in wages. I would like to know from the President of the Treasury Board whether this provision in respect of the 60 days is to be put into effect before these increases are paid. If this is the case, then the 102,000 members of the armed forces and not less than 60,000 others in the civil service will not receive their retroactive pay until after January 1.
As I understand the legislation in respect of the social development tax, no exemption is to be made in respect of money received in 1969 that was earned in 1968. There was nothing in the speech of the Minister of Finance or in the legislation that would permit payments made in 1969 on moneys earned in 1968 to be exempt from that surcharge. I personally know of three agreements that have been signed by the government with its staff. I also know, although only by press reports, of an increase for the armed forces. I receive letters every day asking whether the government is going to hold to that 60 day provision before the money is paid and whether it will not be paid until after January 1 of next year. I know that many members of the House of Commons have received similar letters.
I raise this matter now in respect of the three contracts which I know have been signed and the increase which I know has been agreed to for the armed forces. I ask the minister whether this money will be paid before December 31 or whether it is to be held until after January 1 when the 2 per
Supply-Treasury Board cent surcharge will be collectible from the personnel of the armed forces and civil servants on money they earned in 1968. A question on this matter was asked of the Minister of Finance last Friday, I believe. The minister would not give an answer. Will the President of the Treasury Board now get up on his feet and say what the situation is and what he will authorize? I ask him not to be a stinker and charge civil servants next year on money they earned this year.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether the President of the Treasury Board will agree not to be a stinker. I am not asking him for any commitment which he may not be able to keep.
I should like to spend the few minutes until six o'clock raising two matters related to collective bargaining concerning which the Treasury Board has the responsibility of representing the employer in the public service. I wish to say first of all, as we said at the time when the relevant bills which later became law were before this chamber, that we are delighted that collective bargaining in the public service has finally been introduced. We are delighted with some of the progress which has been made in respect of the certification of bargaining units. I would say, however, that we were disappointed at the incredibly bad way in which the Treasury Board approached actual negotiations, of which the negotiations with the postal unions were perhaps the most striking example.
Having had some years of experience in negotiations I have not known anything more reprehensible on the part of an employer than the refusal for a period of months to make any monetary offer to the other side. When one sits down to negotiate in private industry, even if the demands of the union are considered outrageous by the employer, no objective employer refuses to make an offer on monetary matters for a period of months. If he did so, the employer would be called a stinker and a good many other applicable and relevant names.
This is exactly what happened in the case of the negotiations with the postal employees. My information is that this has happened during other negotiations although not over as protracted a period as in the case of the postal employees. The period has been long enough, however, that the public service organizations concerned are becoming terribly upset about the situation.

November 18, 1968
Supply*-Treasury Board
There is another item in this regard about which I should like to protest. Anyone who looks at this objectively ought to protest no matter on which side of the house he sits. During negotiations with one section of the public service-I forget exactly which one but I believe it had relation to seaway employees; this was during the election campaign-the President of the Treasury Board and the Prime Minister on separate occasions made public declarations that in their view the 6 per cent which was recommended by one of the conciliators or the conciliation board itself was a proper and fair settlement. What that means is that the head or the employer, being the Prime Minister, said to the board concerned in respect of negotiations that this was the limit beyond which it could not go. When the government is the employer and it does that in the course of negotiations it is really subverting the negotiation process. It is actually destroying any meaningful collective bargaining. What is the use of a public servants' organization asking for more if the Prime Minister and the President of the Treasury Board lay down a declaration that it cannot be any more?
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
This kind of behaviour in respect of the postal service employees and in respect of the employees of the seaway authority, to which I have just referred, makes a mockery of the collective bargaining process and underlines what some of us said during the hearings of the joint committee. It was said, particularly by my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and myself, that the government was not really prepared to accept the implications of genuine collective bargaining because the government was still going to act as it did before the collective bargaining was introduced, as an authority making unilateral decisions. That is what is meant when the head of the government declares that a certain level of wage increase is fair and adequate. That lays down the law and the people who are concerned in negotiations cannot go any farther.
It is my hope that during the remaining negotiations and any future negotiations this attitude on the part of the government will not show itself and that the negotiators at the negotiating table will not be subject to these open declarations. They will, no doubt, have instructions from the President of the Treasury Board and from the cabinet, which is perfectly legitimate. They are the employers. If Doug Love negotiates on behalf of the

Treasury Board, the employer, he will naturally have instructions from those to whom he is responsible, as is the case in respect of any other negotiations, but a public declaration by the Prime Minister makes it impossible for any negotiations to take place. Let Mr. Love present the arguments as to why it is unjust, unfair, undesirable, improper, uneconomical, dangerous, or whatever else he wants to say, to go beyond a certain point. That is legitimate collective bargaining. He will have his instructions from the Treasury Board.
The President of the Treasury Board and the Prime Minister should not come out on the public platform and say the government will not go beyond such and such a point, because collective bargaining is not real unless the people on both sides of the table feel they have the opportunity to present their reasons and have a genuine exchange of ideas with some give and take. The collective bargaining process becomes impossible when you lay down the law away from the collective bargaining table. There is no need for this. I suggest it is merely an expression of authoritarianism that has no place in collective bargaining.
The other matter I want to raise, which is equally disturbing, if not more so, is that during the joint committee sessions on various bills relative to the status of public servants and the collective bargaining process it was pointed out-I remember doing so on several	occasions-that	when the law
excludes from the collective bargaining area such fields as classification, promotion, demotion, job descriptions, job evaluations and all the rest, it takes away from the public service an immensely important area for collective bargaining. The fact that we were right has since been proven in a number of cases.
Some time before the collective bargaining process became law the Treasury Board engaged in a reclassification of the public service. This has been going on throughout the piece until today. A good many employees of the government have been reclassified and literally thousands have been red-circled. This means they have been told they now have a new classification lower than the classification which they formerly held at a salary rate higher than the salary rate of the new classification. Therefore they are frozen at their present salary rates and are not entitled to the increases which their organizations have now negotiated or are now negotiating. They will remain frozen until such time as
November 18, 1968

the salary for the lower classification is increased to the salary they now receive in the higher classification.
I have had numerous letters, telegrams and personal conversations which indicated that literally thousands of civil servants have not received any of these increases and, in some cases, were even refused increases that went back to a date before they were reclassified. This is really reprehensible. I do not know whether hon. members and the President of the Treasury Board understand me. Perhaps I did not make myself clear. If reclassification or red-circling took place in October of 1968, let us say, this was made retroactive to October 1, 1967, so that the people concerned did not even get the increase applicable to their classification for the year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: SUGGESTED DEDUCTION OF RESIDENTIAL TAXES AND RENTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the feasibility
Income Tax
of allowing residential taxes on owner-occupied homes and rental of accommodation of tenants to be deductible from federal personal income tax.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to introduce a motion designed to come to the relief of the overburdened Canadian taxpayer. The motion which you have read I would like to read again. It reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the feasibility of allowing residential taxes on owner-occupied homes and rental of accommodation of tenants to be deductible from federal personal income tax.
I should like to say that I fully endorse the declaration of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that the government of Canada should create a just society for all Canadians. This is the basic principle underlying my motion.
The purpose of my motion is to bring once again to the attention of the government, and especially to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), the urgent need to ease the great burden of the Canadian taxpayer who is not only heavily taxed but in some cases is the victim of double taxation. It is my opinion, which I believe may be shared by all hon. members and by many fellow citizens, that both the home owners as well as tenants in rooming houses and apartments deserve fairer consideration by the Minister of Finance.
The present taxation system has been called in some quarters a flagrant ease of double taxation in that the federal personal income tax is a tax on municipal taxes as well as on personal income. The United States recognizes the inequity of such a practice and therefore has introduced a law which permits home owners to deduct municipal taxes from income for federal income tax purposes. It even goes much farther. It allows payments on mortgages on homes of citizens also to be considered an exemption for income tax purposes.
During the past few years many representations have been made to the federal government, to the Carter Royal Commission on Taxation and very recently to the federal task force on housing and urban development headed by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer), urging the government to adopt a similar practice. Repeatedly over the past several years, the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities has also appealed in its submissions to the federal and provincial governments recommending the deduction of municipal taxes from personal income

November 18, 1968
Income Tax
tax and even the deduction of home mortgage interest payments.
In the manoeuvring to give Canadians a new tax system it is obvious that there is growing concern and dissatisfaction among the people of Canada at the fact that the problem of municipal taxation is not being given the attention it properly deserves. I believe it is imperative that the Minister of Finance along with his provincial counterparts give this serious matter deeper study and favourable consideration.
House and home stand at the centre of people's lives. Proper shelter means security. It also means independence and privacy. These are the things which we need in our daily life. I believe it is also time to insist that the social aspects of housing be among the determinants of economic policy in our country instead of always being its unfortunate victim. In the present condition of our economy the ownership of a private home is a heavy financial burden for the ordinary Canadian wage earner. After paying an average of $26,000 to $28,000 for a home in a city like Toronto and after paying all kinds of provincial and federal taxes, our citizens are additionally burdened with an ever-increasing municipal tax year after year.
I would also like to appeal to the Minister of Finance to take into account the burdens of the municipal authorities. They are an essential part of our system of government, and I believe it is only fair that they should be given a fairer deal. Canadian municipal authorities find themselves forced to expand their public utility activities. Expenditures on education, transportation, health services, and social welfare have steadily increased. This investment in human resources is a great burden both on the property owner and the people who live in apartment houses and have to pay very high rents. Many Canadian citizens are asking themselves to what extent they should, through municipal taxation, continue to finance education, health services, social welfare services, police and fire protection, and other kinds of services. These benefits which are provided by our municipal authorities are not only shared by local residents but also by government institutions. Therefore it is quite appropriate, I believe, that these expenditures should be financed partly, if not as much as possible, by both the federal and the provincial governments.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
We have heard many times, and especially recently we have read in the newspapers,

about the number of briefs that are being presented to the federal task force on housing and urban development to the effect that the housing shortage is not only acute in Canada but also a crisis. I believe that to meet this crisis the federal government, and especially the Minister of Finance, should give assistance to home owners and potential home owners. I realize that any effort to curb taxes, to protect the soundness of the dollar from inflation, is important. Inflation has eroded the security of many of our people who depend upon a fixed income. The heavy load placed upon most property taxpayers produces some very unhappy results. Older people with limited retirement incomes are left to exist on small pensions, and many of them are greatly harmed. They denied themselves in earlier years many things in order to pay off mortgaged homes. Now they find themselves faced with ever heavier municipal taxes year after year.
We have been told that older people would be better off in apartments, but many of them have no choice and no chance to move out of their own homes. They have to stay there. They have to cope with the problems of maintenance, and also, they face a rise in taxes	whenever they make substantial
improvements. Tenants in apartment houses also face increases in rents whenever municipal taxes rise. As municipal taxes go up, costs of maintenance soar and the tenants in apartment houses are forced to pay higher rents.
I realize that it is not an easy task to work out techniques that will give municipalities more revenues without raising property taxes. However, this is an objective which demands an effort by the responsible ministers of our federal government and especially by their senior advisers. I realize also that taxation should be on a basis that is equitable for all. I understand, too, the concern of the royal commission on taxation when it states that it is difficult to devise a system of credits for property taxes against personal income tax liabilities that would be equitable between those who own their homes and those who rent from others. In spite of the difficulty, we should do everything possible to solve this problem.
By adopting this motion hon. members will not only ease the tax burden but also stimulate the Canadian economy. I believe that all of us in this house desire to give the taxpayers of Canada a long overdue break. The load of the Canadian taxpayer has been made heavier by a succession of increased taxes at
November 18, 1968

the federal, provincial and municipal levels. Finance ministers have even devised new names for all kinds of new taxes, the latest one being the 2 per cent social development tax. The steadily rising cost of living also adds to the burden of the wage earner and especially the family bread winner to provide decent accommodation and the other necessities of life.
The matter of taxation in Canada is an urgent issue. I know it is complicated as well as being a vital instrument in our society and form of government. The royal commission on taxation, under the chairmanship of Mr. Carter and other experts, has revealed these difficult tax problems. "We have been promised a government statement on the report of the Carter royal commission on taxation but this has not been forthcoming as yet. I realize, as I have said, that it is not an easy problem. However, we must deal with the situation now because it is urgent.
When the federal government introduced income taxes it was felt that a basic deduction of $1,000 for a single person and $2,000 for a married wage earner represented the basic necessities of life. However, these exemptions are completely inadequate today. I am sure all hon. members will agree with me on that point. In presenting this motion to the house, I know that it is an attempt to amend the income tax but I feel this motion will recommend itself to all hon. members. By supporting this motion they will make it possible not only for the residents of owner occupied homes but also for people who live in apartment houses and boarding houses to claim an exemption for personal income tax. Therefore, in the same vein of thought I am sure hon. members will feel that justice is being done. I believe these people deserve this break.	'
The government will also recognize by this move a basic social need. Such an exemption would encourage home ownership which is the goal and dream of many Canadians. The dream is for a decent home in a sound environment. This is the best place for a man to raise his family. It is the duty of a democratic government, I believe, especially one which has declared its purpose to work for the establishment of a just society, to provide for its citizens decent housing at reasonable cost. As well as the moral, economic and policical implications of inadequate housing, congested living, slums and the burden of taxation, there are also many mental and physical health implications, as well as the harmful effects of air pollution in our industrialized
Income Tax
urban centres. These problems must be dealt with too, and during the discussion of this motion I should like to add that I believe a special federal department of housing and environmental affairs should be created without further delay.
The exemption I propose in the motion would also stimulate our economy by encouraging the buying of more and better houses. This would also alleviate our rising unemployment problem. Above all, it would enable our citizens to lead better lives and would provide them with a greater chance for the fulfillment of their human potential. I appeal to all hon. members to support and pass this motion. Such action would ease the intolerable load of taxation that is burdening the taxpayers of Canada. The people in owner occupied homes as well as people living in apartment houses and boarding houses would benefit in many ways if all hon. members would accept this motion which I have proposed again in this session of parliament. Our opportunities in this house to reduce taxation are rare. We must not neglect the present opportunity.
