I rise with some concern, Mr. Speaker, because I do believe that if it is possible for us to have a just society, then this just society must result from the directions of the government. However, with the greatest respect, I say that I do not believe in the phrase "a just society" because I believe it is an expression that has no meaning. I should like to place my emphasis, therefore, on what might be called the quality of life. I feel this is what we are concerned with, the quality of life of all Canadians; it is in this area that we should be genuinely concerned.
During his remarks the hon. member mentioned that owning one's own home is becoming an impossibility. Certainly this is something that we should investigate. I recall very vividly that in my maiden speech I said that owning one's own home was becoming an impossibility. In other words, the leadership that we had expected, and I think rightly expected, to come from this government has not been forthcoming. We find that we have a task force that is pussyfooting around the country. As a matter of fact, even in this just society the task force did not want to come to Hamilton. I had to indicate that Hamiltonians were interested in the task force and that it should come to Hamilton to look into the housing situation.

November 18, 1S68
Income Tax
When I heard the hon. member's motion it sort of rang a bell. The motion reads in part: That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give immediate consideration to the feasibility of allowing residential taxes on owner-occupied homes-
I remember stumping the streets in 1965 at a time when this party had a program which indicated we were cognizant of the situation. We said at that time that if we formed the government we would allow an exemption of $500 from income taxes for this purpose. Therefore I have risen to support the hon. member who is concerned about rising taxes. In this just society we have just had the raising of taxes by a further 2 per cent, the so-called social development tax. I am sure I speak on behalf of almost everyone in this house when I say that hon. members would support this motion because it is important that we give some relief to the many people who are being strangled as a result of high taxes at all levels of government.
I realize that the hon. member has carried his motion much farther. Even though the Carter royal commission says there is a problem, the hon. member says we should not only give some consideration to the owner-occupier but should move into the area of rental accommodation. This should be considered too, and how just this is if we are going to move into a just society. At the same time we are talking about the quality of life and in many instances, because of peculiar circumstances, we see the effect of housing on this sort of thing but it is disregarded.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that there is no question that housing is one of the most important priorities we have to face. Briefs are being presented from all parts of the country to emphasize its urgency and I am sure hon. members are receiving letters from all across Canada, not only from their constituents, on the subject.
When I think of a house, Mr. Speaker, I think not only of a roof over my head but of what the house itself contains. The hon. member has already expressed more articulately than I what I am trying to say, but when I think of a house I think of the fact that the provision of accommodation means a reduction in juvenile delinquency. I think it improves marital relations. I also think of a general reduction in crime.

Most important of all, Mr. Speaker, I think of the ghetto type of living about which people in other countries have become quite concerned. Where grievances lie dormant for months or years we find they reach the stage of being beyond solution, so that the solution itself becomes a problem. This in turn leads to riots, the type of social disorder that we in Canada certainly do not want and cannot afford.
I commend the hon. member for bringing forward this resolution. I am a new member and I understood him to say that he was bringing it forward again; it is good that he does so because I am pleased to stand and support it. At one t:me it appeared that we were interested only in the low income earner who was in a terrible situation as far as housing was concerned. We now find, at least as far as I am concerned, that no matter what part of the country one lives in one has to make at least $9,000 or $10,000 before one can become a home owner. Therefore we have moved our consideration from the low income earner to the average income earner.
Most people thought that the government had given weighty consideration to our housing crisis. As I understand it, the former minister of labour initiated a symposium on housing. This symposium travelled around the country seeking information. But surely, Mr. Speaker, they knew what was going on. We are now awaiting with great expectations the present task force's return.
I too, Mr. Speaker, like my hon. friend, think that housing is a matter of great consequence. As a matter of fact, one of the briefs that was presented stated;
However, with the growth of the country, the present dire need for housing our citizens and the many diversified problems involved in meeting that challenge, it is the contention of our association that such a task requires the undivided attention of a minister of housing to lead and direct the federal effort in solving the many questions arising in housing and urban development.
The brief goes on to state:
We believe, too, that the job of co-ordinating those activities which influence housing matters being carried out by other government departments such as-
Listen to the list, Mr. Speaker.
-the Treasury Board, Department of Finance, Labour, Manpower and Immigration, Transport, Consumer Affairs, Veterans Affairs, requires the full time services of a housing minister as does the federal housing relationship with the various provincial and municipal governments.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, one can see that this is no easy task. The job does not call for
November 18, 1968

the services of one minister who has one or two portfolios, approaching the question with the attitude: Let us face the problem because the people are screaming for housing.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to stand and support my hon. friend's motion. We in this party sincerely believe that housing should not be beyond the reach of the Canadian people. This is why we believe we should move in the area of assisting municipalities to reduce the cost of land and services. We should be where the action is so that people who have average incomes or below can afford a home. This is a great necessity. We should take cognizance of those with below average incomes because this is where the trouble may start, as I have tried to indicate earlier. We have to think of individual home ownership. I should like to think that this is everybody's dream in the long run, to own one's own home. Thank goodness I was able to buy one ten years ago because I could not buy one today. Perhaps there are many here who do not yet own a home and cannot afford one either.
We also have to be concerned about low rental housing, housing research, housing construction methods, the cost of municipal services, row housing, co-operatives and condominiums.
I do not think I should take up any more time of the house, Mr. Speaker, except to say this. I think the hon. member has projected something of great consequence this afternoon. It is to be hoped that all hon. members will look upon it as favourably as he did in order that the phrase about which we hear so much these days, "the just society", will at long last mean that yes, we are in fact living in a just society.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish that I and other members of this group could support this motion because I have no doubt at all that the intent of the motion moved by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) is to help the overburdened taxpayer. We all know that in many cases the overburdened taxpayer is in very serious jeopardy now. However, as spokesman for my party on this measure, Mr. Speaker, I cannot possibly support the motion because it does violence to the major principle that should underlie all taxation, that is, the principle of taxation according to ability to pay. Indeed, it stands poor Mr. Carter right on his head. Although the Carter report has been cited this afternoon, the one principle that underlies the Carter report is that
29180-182^
Income Tax
people should be taxed according to their income and ability to pay.
This proposal, Mr. Speaker, does not do that at all. According to this proposal the people who have the best houses and pay the most taxes get the biggest rebate. The people less able to pay and whose taxes proportionately eat up a much larger share of their income receive much less relief than the wealthy. That does not fit in with my concept of a just society.
I know that is not the intention of the hon. member for Parkdale, Mr. Speaker, but unfortunately that is the effect of his motion. This is why our party cannot support it. Our whole effort and energy have been directed toward the premise that it is not terribly important how much you pay in taxes; what is important is what you have left to live on after your taxes are paid. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, this motion would lighten the load of the taxpayer in proportion to the amount his income increases. This takes a bigger share of the local taxes away from him than from the lower income taxpayer, through the federal agency. We do not regard that a fair way of doing things.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) spoke of the importance of giving fair consideration to the taxpayer, and he emphasized that it should be fair. I do not consider this measure to be fair, and I think we ought to reject it and look for other ways of doing what is intended to be done. In other words, this measure of relief has no relation to the income of the person who is to be relieved of paying taxes.
Reference has been made to the Federation of Mayors and Municipalities. I have in my hand one of the resolutions that was moved by that body this year, and I read from it as follows:
-Resolved that, for the purposes of obtaining relief from the burden of the property tax, provincial assistance should be provided which would contain the following characteristics as basic principles :
-both tenants and owners to benefit;
-assistance directly related to the property tax;
-the assistance to be of highest benefit to low-income persons.
If one only reads to the second item, "assistance directly related to the property tax," the hon. member for Parkdale can say, "You see, that is exactly what I am doing." But if one reads the third item, "the assistance to be of highest benefit to the low-income persons,"

November 18, 1968
Income Tax
he finds that the hon. member did not go far enough in dealing with this set of propositions.
In order to bring relief to those most needing it, the biggest benefits ought to be made available to low income people. Such would not be the case with the hon. member's notice of motion.
I now wish to talk about that part of the notice of motion which refers to the feasibility of allowing residential taxes on owner-occupied homes and rental of accommodation of tenants to be deductible from federal personal income tax. The meaning of that is not clear. I know what the hon. member for Parkdale intended, but lawyers have a habit of not reading minds. They look at cold print. The hon. member's motion does not indicate whether the benefit under the federal income tax is to go to the renter or the tenant. Who is to be forgiven? I know what the hon. member intended, but this measure I submit does not indicate what he intended. I think many lawyers might argue about the meaning of this measure and not arrive at a clear understanding, simply because of the way it is worded.
If we are to ask the federal government to help municipalities I think the best and most obvious way to do that is for us to get busy and act on the housing needs of the municipalities in a more co-operative way than has been the case to date. When I attended the federal housing conference in Toronto two or three weeks ago I heard over and over again that housing is no problem if one has money. Only if one has insufficient money will he have difficulty obtaining a home.
If the federal government is to assist in the housing needs of the municipalities it ought to follow the advice of members of more than one housing delegation, who said that we in this country require large scale and diversified building. I know that many people in the country would love to own their own home; while on the other hand there are many others who do not want to do so. We live in a mobile society and a quarter of our families move every year. People who move, and young people in particular, do not want to be burdened with owning a home. Rental accommodation is better suited to their needs. I have spent half my life in homes that I or my family owned and the other half in rented accommodation, and from my experience the

type of work one does will influence the decision as to whether one wishes to own a home or rent one.
In this country we need both more owner-occupied homes and more rental homes. The need for rental accommodation is fully as great in Canada as the need for private homes. Like the hon. member for Parkdale, I know of many cases, tragic cases, where old people cannot leave their large, old homes because they cannot afford to obtain alternative accommodation. I do not think the best way to help these people is by forgiving them their municipal taxes. That would not help them obtain a new home. We must provide more suitable homes for senior citizens, no matter whether they are separate homes, terraces, or, as in the case of Vancouver, separate homes that are incorporated in an apartment block. All these types are needed.
Ottawa can help the municipalities in a practical way by aiding people in the matter of income. I suggest that our basic income tax exemptions ought to be raised. That would be a much fairer way to help our taxpayers, no matter whether they live in owner-occupied homes or rental accommodation. Raising exemption levels to, say, $2,000 for single persons and $4,000 for married couples would be of immeasurably greater assistance to our overburdened taxpayers than the forgiving of their municipal taxes. I submit that our taxpayers could be helped far more if Ottawa were to raise basic income tax exemptions than if they were forgiven their municipal taxes. That would be a fairer way of doing it.
We cannot consider the question of how to help our taxpayers from one angle only. Housing is a vital need in our nation. If our municipalities are to have a larger tax base, they must have more houses from which to raise taxes. More houses mean greater municipal revenues. We must not forget that.
No doubt other hon. members wish to speak on this measure. I have made the points I wanted to make. I do not want the hon. member to think that we have not considered our position carefully. We approve of his trying to help the overburdened taxpayer, but we say with regret that this form of help will not lead to the just society. On the contrary, it will widen the gap between those who have much and those who have little. Consequently we cannot support this motion.

subtopic: SUGGESTED DEDUCTION OF RESIDENTIAL TAXES AND RENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this notice of motion I wish to say briefly that I concur
November 18, 1988

with the principle of the motion, subject to certain reservations. I concur with the views of the hon. members for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) and Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz). It is my view that this motion ought to be considered along with a total review of our entire taxation system. Only that way can matters be made more equitable for all concerned.
It is a common saying that a man's home is his castle, and this applies equally to the home of an owner and to that of a tenant. It is regrettable that in our day and age to keep up this castle is more difficult than ever, mostly owing to the exorbitant tax rates presently being levied against real property. That directly effects the homeowner, and indirectly the tenants to whom tax increases are transmitted by means of higher rents.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
These increases in realty taxes impose a great burden on all citizens, particularly on our senior citizens who are presently struggling on savings based on earnings of yesteryear. For these people, many of whom live in my riding of Toronto-High Park, the situation is difficult to cope with. To a large extent they must rely on small savings and assistance from their children to supplement the meagre old age security assistance they presently receive. Surely, after all they have done, they should be entitled to a better fate. Permission enabling them to deduct realty taxes from income would certainly be a step in the right direction. As to the comment of the previous speaker about elderly people who own large homes, I should like to point out that in many cases these homes have great sentimental value; their occupants are reluctant to leave them and I think they should be entitled to stay in these homes for which they worked and for which they helped to pay.
Permission to deduct realty taxes should also be given to those in the lower and middle income groups who are also overtaxed. If we consider this matter from a practical point of view, it becomes clear that this realty tax is actually a form of double taxation. Consider first, the residential home owner. The realty taxes he or she pays come from net income received, an income which is taxable federally. So, technically speaking, a home owner is paying tax upon tax.
A tenant finds himself in a somewhat similar position, since the rent he pays is in large measure dependant on the landlord's overhead, a major portion of which is constituted by realty taxes. Under our present income tax structure a landlord must declare the rents he
Income Tax
receives as income, and this income is, in turn, taxable. But remember: the tenant who pays the rent is paying it out of his net income, which has to be declared for income tax purposes. In essence therefore he is paying tax on tax, as is the home owner. Because of such inequities it is becoming increasingly difficult for a citizen to acquire and, in due course, to own shelter for himself and his family-a basic necessity of life.
Permission to deduct property taxes from income would, I firmly believe, lead to an increase in home construction, encourage home ownership and allow municipalities to raise much needed revenue to meet their ever-growing obligations, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz). In addition, an extra incentive would be given to home owners to improve and repair their premises and make them more beautiful for the benefit of the community. The step I propose would bring taxation more closely in line with ability to pay.
It is sometimes argued that to allow the deduction of residential taxes would normally be of greater benefit to the more affluent taxpayers than to others. In order to counteract this argument, which I consider to have merit, I would respectfully recommend a deduction ceiling of $750. This would eliminate any advantage which might otherwise be derived by more affluent taxpayers. It is my submission that over and above a certain basic amount necessary for a shelter in which to. house a family, the added cost is strictly for frills and luxuries.
I further submit that notwithstanding arguments to the contrary there would not, in fact, be a revenue loss but in the long run a revenue gain, since the money saved by the taxpayer would be spent elsewhere to assist the economy, and because in many instances persons who have so far not made complete disclosure of rental revenue would be encouraged or obliged to do so.
In addition to supporting this motion I would recommend the deduction from income of interest payable on mortgage payments as they pertain to residential property. A landowner who rents his property is already entitled to such a benefit, and in view of the fact that the benefit is transmitted to the tenant, the residential home owner should, in equity, be allowed the same privilege.
I should like to give hon. members a simple illustration. Let us assume that A sells a house to B for $30,000. The buyer does not have sufficient funds in cash to pay for such a

November 18, 1968
Income Tax
home, so he gives A $10,000 cash and a $20,000 mortgage. Subsequently, A has to buy a house to shelter his own family. He buys one from C at a price similar to that which he has been promised. Since he received only $10,000 from B, he cannot pay the whole amount at once, but places a down payment of $10,000 and in turn gives C a $20,000 mortgage.
According to our present taxation system, A has to declare the interest received on mortgage payments from B, but he is not entitled to deduct interest he is paying on the mortgage equivalent to the one he is paying with respect to the property he bought from C. This shows how inequitable the present system is, and I submit that this interest should be deductible.
Based on these considerations, it is my humble opinion that this house should give immediate consideration to-
(a)	allowing residential taxes on owner-occupied homes to be deducted from federal income tax, up to a ceiling of $750
(b)	allowing tenants to deduct the cost of rental accommodation for federal income tax purposes
(c)	permitting deduction of mortgage interest from personal income tax.
I feel this would alleviate a portion of the heavy tax burden now imposed on taxpayers.

speechtext:
In this resolution the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) proposes that residential taxes, and in certain cases rentals, be deductible from federal personal income tax. Since the second part of the resolution dealing with deduction of rentals is not at all clear to me, I shall merely deal with the first portion regarding deduction of residential taxes.
I see this proposal as having two purposes. One would be to relieve the heavy burden of taxes carried by those who own homes, and the second would be to serve as an incentive to home ownership and to the building of homes for Canadians. Although I agree that residential taxes are a heavy burden I do not think that this is the proper remedy. I certainly agree with the previous speaker, that municipal taxes, residential taxes, school and other land taxes are completely inequitable, unjust, and completely out of step with modern taxation reforms.
November 18, 1968

There are instances, such as those already illustrated in this debate where a person who has improved his land, who has tried to make his home a nicer place in which to live, is penalized by more taxes, whereas a person who allows his house to become run down, to become a slum, pays less tax. Worse than that, take the case of a man who tears down a lot of older homes, sometimes nice homes, and turns the land into a parking lot. He will have his taxes reduced while he waits for the local municipality to introduce a road program or construction program from which he can make a great capital gain by speculating in the land.
If a man clears land and leaves it vacant his municipal tax is lowered. But his neighbour, who improves his home, possibly by building an addition to it to house a larger family, or by building a garage, is penalized because he must pay higher taxes. I agree that residential taxes are extremely unjust, but I do not think the remedy lies in allowing them to be written off as deductions against federal income tax. This would bring about the inequities which the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) mentioned.
I believe the real remedy lies in changing the taxation system. Many suggestions have been made. Some people think municipal services should be paid for through user charges. Others suggest a site value tax, based on the purpose for which land is to be used rather than on tax charges for additions or for new buildings.
Neither do I think the second purpose of the resolution, which is to serve as an incentive for new housing programs, is the proper solution. As the minister in charge of housing said the other day, if we have to apply further subsidies or raise taxes in Canada to alleviate the housing problem we will not really be solving that problem.
I submit that the only way we can really help potential homeowners is by bringing down the cost of homes. Mass production techniques and new technology have been applied to almost all consumer products on the market, but not to house building. Washing machines, refrigerators and automobiles are manufactured through mass production techniques, but until recently homes have been built by old and very costly methods. In this connection I refer to this article which appeared in the Montreal Star of September
Income Tax
24, concerning a new house building technique developed in California:
A computer-directed machine that can build prefabricated walls at the rate of 20 feet a minute, automatically sizing, cutting and nailing the lumber, has been developed in Fresno, California, by three lumber company executives.
The device at M. Kellner and Son Lumber Co. can construct the interior and exterior walls for an average-size two-bedroom house in about 20 minutes. Walls for 500 homes can be built in a week.
It goes on to point out that by using this method costs can be reduced to a great extent.
Other suggestions have been submitted to the task force on housing. I take issue with the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) who said that the task force is not doing a proper job. We must reserve judgment until it brings in its report, and until the government acts on that report. One of the briefs submitted to the task force when it visited Montreal also pointed out that great savings can be made in house building through the introduction of new technology and mass production techniques. If we really want to help the house building industry, if we want to help people in the lower and middle income brackets to have homes they can afford, we must do it through new technology and mass production.

Mr. Chairman, at six o'clock when the time was drawn to my attention, I was literally in the middle of a sentence.
November 18, 1968

Supply-Treasury Board I could not tell you the sentence but I do remember the subject matter. At the time I was dealing with the red circling of a good many employees in the public service, and I had reached the point where I was drawing the attention of the committee and of the President of the Treasury Board to the fact that not only is there the red circling but in many cases, and so far as I have been able to find out in literally thousands of cases, the red circling which was made, say in the fall of this year, was made retroactive to a year earlier.
I really cannot see any justification at all for that. Its effect has been to deprive employees of back pay to which they would otherwise have been entitled. We might take this example-a hypothetical example, but it describes the actual situation. The reclassification in a given situation was completed, let us saw, in October 1967, and was made retroactive to October 1, 1966. In the meantime a collective agreement was arrived at between the applicable organization and the government in which there was an increase of "x" percentage dated back to October 1, 1966. Because the red circling was also made retroactive to October 1, 1966 the employee who was red circled did not even get the increase applicable to the classification in which he worked and was employed for the preceding year.
I am astonished and outraged by that kind of behaviour. If I have misunderstood the situation or if I am misrepresenting it I assure the President of the Treasury board that that misrepresentation is not deliberate and he may correct me; but I do not think I am wrong. What possible explanation can there be for this; what right has an employer to say in October 1967 that, despite the fact that the employee worked in a certain class all through the 12 months from October 1966 to October 1967, he will not receive the increase that has been made applicable to that 12 month period and that he is frozen, not at the rate as of October 1, 1967 but at the rate as of October 1, 1966 and thereby loses the increase to which he is entitled.
For the life of me I really cannot understand what justification there can possibly be for that. If a poor fellow or woman is to be frozen, then let it be at the rate applicable at the date on which the red circling takes place, and not set back as in many cases a full year. From information I have been given, some post office employees and some customs employees have lost in some cases $200 or $300 and even more in back pay to which


otherwise they would have been entitled. This is really indescribably bad labour relations, and it is possible only for an employer as strong as is the government. There is no need for such a scrooge-like attitude toward employees.
When the legislation was before the standing committee, then before this committee and this chamber I appreciated there was some reason for the insistence on the part of the government that classification and promotion cannot be made fully a part of collective bargaining. As I recall the reasoning, it was that the merit system on which it was hoped appointment to the public service and promotion within the public service would be based, made it necessary that there be objective rules laid down by the public service commission, and objective criteria applied in appointments through examination and in promotion through examination, and that therefore the merit system could not be allowed to come under attack or be eroded by the provisions in respect of security and the like that must be considered in ordinary collective agreements.
I speak from memory, but as I believe I said at the time, and say now, I can see some validity in the wish to retain the merit system and not let it become subject to the ordinary collective bargaining limitation; but that does not mean that the organization representing the employees should have no say whatever in classification and promotion procedures. This does not mean that it is impossible for the employer, in this case the government, to consult with the organization representing the public employees in order to give them an opportunity to make representations about the classification and reclassification, and to give them an opportunity to do this before the reclassification becomes a fait accompli, because once it is done, and it is necessary to go through the grievance procedure and appeal procedure before the public service commission, there is nothing very much that will be done then.
I am certain it is an uncivilized procedure-and I use that word deliberately because I think it is uncivilized-for a big employer to say that it has the power to make the classifications and reclassifications, and is going to do it, and that the employee must take it even retroactively for a year if the employer so decides. That is not civilized labour relations. In a civilized situation there is no reason why the organization concerned should not be consulted and informed before
November 18, 1968

the reclassification and red circling becomes a fact, so that the organization would be in a position to put its case before the representatives of the Treasury Board. Had this been the case, perhaps the kind hard heart which faces me across the aisle might have agreed not to impose the retroactivity of the red circling. I have known him to be kind; I have also known him to be hard hearted. Perhaps if the organization had caught him in one of his kind moods he might have seen the injustice involved in the red circling of people retroactively for a whole year.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
I say to the President of the Treasury Board that the reason the collective bargaining has worked so far is not because he and his associates have done what they should have done in respect of the public service collective bargaining process, because from my observation they have broken a good many basic rules of collective bargaining. I indicated they broke the rules in respect of making some offer to the people on the other side, as soon as negotiations began, so that movement could start early. In the case of the postal service employees, if my memory serves me right, it was some seven months before they made the first offer. This is almost an invitation to strike. When you keep people waiting for seven months before making them any offer at all, the bitterness that develops among the rank and file makes it impossible for anyone to keep them from striking. By that kind of collective bargaining you invite disputes of a serious kind.
The employer in this case, I suggest, also broke the basic rules of collective bargaining by laying down a ukase as to the amount the seaway employees would get. The Prime Minister stated that 6 per cent was fair, and the government would not give any more. He made the statement while negotiations were taking place. In my opinion the government also broke the basic rules of collective bargaining by imposing retroactive red circling without discussion or consultation with the organizations. Even with discussion and consultation it was wrong to do this.
The reason the collective bargaining process has worked as well as it has so far in the public service is not due to the proper behaviour on the part of the government, although a lot of it has been proper. In many cases the basic rules of collective bargaining were broken. It has worked as well as it has because public service organizations have not yet developed the militancy that unions usually develop, and because in the early stages
Supply-Treasury Board of collective bargaining, even in private industry let alone in the public service, unions tend to be a little more timid and careful.
I warn the government that, as the unions become more certain of themselves and as they gain confidence in their capacity to face their employer across the bargaining table, instead of having to accept orders and ukases, if the government does not change its attitude toward some of these rules of collective bargaining it will invite a great deal more disruption than we have had in the past.
Strikes in services like government services usually take place as the result of serious circumstances, and they occur only when the employer also has made mistakes. In the government service we have responsible employees and responsible leaders. I am using careful words. I am not saying strikes occur when the employer alone has made mistakes; I am saying they occur when the employer and the other side have made mistakes. In this case there is no excuse for the employer making mistakes. The government and its huge civil service ought to be able to research the situation so as to avoid mistakes.
Let me repeat my warning. If things are not changed, then serious difficulties will occur in the future. They need not occur. Let me conclude my remarks by even now pleading with the President of the Treasury Board to reverse the decision with regard to the retroactive red circling of employees. There is no justification on any social or moral ground for a person who has worked in a certain class before being red circled not getting an increase applicable to his class for that year. Every employee who was deprived of retroactive pay to which he was entitled suffered a grave injustice. It is not too late for the President of the Treasury Board to persuade his colleagues in cabinet that this injustice should be rectified.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a few observations I should like to make. During our consideration of this item in the estimates. When we are in the committee of supply I sometimes have the feeling that dealing with these estimates is like an ancient tribal ritual greeting spring. It has no real meaning as an examination of the estimates. I only hope that the new structure or procedure of sending the estimates to committees will be more effective. While I recognize the usefulness of using the discussion of estimates as a means of presenting the sort of argument we have heard from members of the N.D.P.- and we have been doing the same thing-I hope that proper use of the committee system will result in a far more meaningful effort.
Let me make several observations in this regard. I should like to consider this whole matter of using the estimates as a gauge of national expenditure. The Leader of the Opposition during our early consideration of the estimates questioned the President of the Treasury Board about the five year projections of spending proposals. After listening carefully to the minister's answers, I think our estimates would have far more meaning and value if the form of the estimates was changed. This form is subject to change, and I recall from my experience as a member of the public accounts committee that a great many useful changes could be made. Surely one change that might well be made is the inclusion with these various estimates of the five year projection in respect of particular votes dealing with specific and committed programs, so that we would see year by year the extent to which these five year projections had been in fact adhered to.

DEBATES	November 18, 1968
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I can give a typical example. We had some questions in the house the other day about an item involving the expenditure of $61 million for the construction of a complex of buildings for the C.B.C. in the Montreal area. I think this information was given in response to a return which had been asked for on written questions. I would like to suggest that there is nobody in this committee who is listening to me now who would be prepared to wager any sizeable amount of money that by the time this particular project is completed its cost will be limited to $61 million. I would be very much surprised if, having in mind the usual changes, it were not much closer to $100 million by the time it is finished.
This is the kind of thing that I think, if we are going to have any meaningful and intelligent examination of specific projects, members of this committee, acting as the people charged by the 20 million people of Canada to examine the spending habits of the government, to see that we are in fact getting good value for our money, and to ascertain what would be the proper priorities to assign to different spending programs, should have an opportunity to examine. This may possibly be somewhat more limited than what the government, the Treasury Board and the cabinet would do, but some effort should be make on our behalf, and information should be given to us so that we could look at these respective programs. Then, in four or five years, we would be able to come to decisions, to evaluate the various proposals, and possibly, when we come to deal with the supply of money to the government, we would be able to exercise a judgment which at the present time I am afraid can only be a stab in the dark.
There may be good and valid reasons why this should not be done. My recollection is that it was Secretary McNamara in the United States who introduced into the department of defence there a budget programming, and a more intelligent and searching look. We heard from the Minister of Finance that he too is now doing this scientifically and that he has computers for the purpose. Talking about tribal rituals, and having in mind what the Minister of Finance has succeeded in doing, I often think that when he came to estimate his budgetary proposals and his deficit he probably slaughtered a chicken and examined its entrails, and this is where he came up with the facts which he gave to this house last fall, and again recently.
November 18, 1968

I would suggest that this is an aspect of the estimates which might well be considered, so that year by year we would have an opportunity of comparing what in fact were the actual expenditures with the projections which had been made. This might well have been applied to the national centre for the performing arts here in Ottawa. Such information might have been given members of this house and, without judging the merits of this or any project, I do think a similar procedure would really make for a more searching and intelligent scrutiny of the bad spending habits of the government-they have a few good ones but most of them are bad-by the members of this house, an opportunity which at the present time they are denied.
I would also like to deal with the aggregate of the amounts we find in these estimates. I listened very carefully to the explanations of the minister that the Treasury Board, at the appropriate time, having heard from the various departments, takes appropriate steps as a result of which the blue book emerges. But, after all, the blue book should be taken as a virtual contract between the government and the people of Canada whom we represent. The details of any good contract are offered for acceptance and consideration. The government offers to do certain things, to provide certain services and certain public works, and the people of Canada, through parliament, agree to pay so much for it. That is the consideration. But what we find is that this contract is broken year after year. Every time supplementary estimates are brought into this house, there is in fact a breach of contract.
I am not suggesting any government, and certainly not this government, is able to anticipate with accuracy and precision that some contingencies may not arise in the future, but when we see the total aggregate of the supplementary estimates which have been brought in, for example over the last five years, I say that surely, when the Treasury Board has with great pains and meticulous care gone through the departmental proposals and come up with the figures in the blue book, we should be entitled to look at them as being a firm contract.
We find that over the last five years over $4 billion was brought in by way of supplementary estimates. In the fiscal year 1963-64 there were five sets of supplementary estimates, from A to E inclusive, totalling $730 million. In 1964-65 there were four sets of supplementary estimates aggregating $900 million. In 1965-66 there were five sets of
Supply-Treasury Board supplementary estimates with a total of approximately $850 million. In 1966-67 there were seven sets of supplementary estimates aggregating $1,200 million. In 1967-68 there were three sets of supplementary estimates aggregating $460 million. As I said, the total is approximately $4,200 million.
This is a practice which has to be reviewed very carefully. What does really happen? Do the departments, being unable to bring in to Treasury Board the full amount of the expenditures they would really like to make, soften the blow by asking for a little less, or allow themselves to be taken down to a little less money, knowing all the time that before the fiscal year is over they are going to come back with requests, through the medium of supplementary estimates, to get the total figure for which they originally asked? If that is the case, then it is just a game which is being played.
There is no certainty about it, and I think that members of this house are entitled to better treatment than this. I point this out more in sorrow than in anger, in the belief that the practice is one which should, and I hope will, be reviewed. If the committee structure works properly, I think there will be adequate opportunity through this means to have a careful study made of these estimates as they are going through, and in fact through an examination of departmental officials committee members should be able to find out if the estimates as produced in the blue book are the total that they expect to receive for the fiscal year.
Then I want to add to that my dislike of another practice, which I think is equally invidious, of adding several hundred million dollars each year under the heading of loans, investments and advances. I am not going to go into the details of this matter, since I have done so before, but I am going to keep on coming back to it as long as I think the practice of the government is wrong.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Quite obviously many of these so-called loans, investments and advances are, in fact, expenditures. They are, in fact, expenditures of the crown and not loans or income producing investments. All one needs to do is to examine some of the items in question, and it becomes absolutely obvious there is not going to be any return to the consolidated revenue fund on moneys lent in this way, other than by subsequent expenditure items which are contained in future appropriations. This is the
2884	COMMONS
Supply-Treasury Board only way the loan is going to be repaid. I may be ignorant of the finer points of government financing, but surely there should be some distinction made between a valid loan made to a crown corporation where there is some hope of repayment, and the kind of expenditure we have seen. I dislike referring to the C.B.C. all the time, but we find a $25 million loan to the C.B.C. and another $35 million loan to the C.B.C. I make mention of these things, Mr. Chairman, because I think they are important, having in mind the problems faced by the ordinary taxpayer today in trying to make ends meet. We have a duty cast upon us to scrutinize as closely as we can the various expenditures. I am not satisfied that the government is putting before us the information we should have. I make this as my annual presentation. If the minister is where he is next year and I am where I am, then I will be coming back again to this subject. I am not an optimist like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. The answer is no. As I assured another hon. member in the house the other day, we are making every effort, as fast as the administrative machinery can accomplish it, to put into the hands of recipients the cheques for retroactive pay. The hon. member for York South, who I am sorry is not here, spoke at some length on the question of the poor or invidious practices of the Treasury Board in conducting collective bargaining negotiations. He referred particularly to two questions; one was the unreasonableness of the Prime Minister and the President of the Treasury Board in announcing, during the currency of negotiations with the seaway workers, a 6 per cent ceiling on increases. The Minister of Transport, under whose department the seaway comes, did at one point make an announcement but the Treasury Board did not. For this reason one might have argued that the remarks of the hon. member for York South were out of order. But even if they had been in order, I am a little surprised, Mr. Chairman, at his logic in defining the actions of one of the parties in the collective bargaining process in making a public statement as to its bargaining position as being unreasonable and illogical, without at the same time requiring the other party to observe a similar line of conduct. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, it is not in the spirit of what the hon. member for York South described as the give and take of the collective bargaining process to endeavour to impose complete freedom of action in relation to public-private negotiations, or in moving from one arena to the other, on the one side without at least a comparable freedom on the other. The hon. member complains it is wrong and unjust for the employer to state his position publicly while the bargaining is going on, yet it seems to be quite reasonable and logical for the employee side to go to the public with its case. I suggest that in this particular instance there should at least be some element of reciprocity observed in the conduct of negotiations.
The hon. member also dealt with the refusal of the government to put on the table a
Supply-Treasury Board wage offer in the case of the postal workers. I think the house will recollect that after some very considerable delay an offer of a pay increase was made. This was somewhat summarily rejected and the strike followed.
The fact of the matter is, Mr. Chairman, that the negotiations had been going on for a very long while. During these negotiations there had been little evidence of the give and take that I suggest is of the essence of collective bargaining. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, it was the failure to make any kind of progress at all on some of the rather minor points that led Treasury Board to be dubious about the value of putting on the table at too early a stage a wage offer that undoubtedly, as subsequent events proved, would have been rejected.
I do not think that one can argue that there is a set timetable, a prescribed ritual, for the conduct of collective bargaining:	it does
depend on the relative willingness of the parties to engage in meaningful negotiations. If for one reason or another this willingness is absent, then perhaps going through a procedure or a series of procedures probably will not advance matters very much. However, Mr. Chairman, I did listen with great interest to his admonitions. If I may use that term. The hon. member has had a great deal of experience in this field, though perhaps on the one side. Certainly my own experience is very limited indeed, but I do profess myself willing to learn, or to try to learn.
The hon. member also made a point about red circling, and explained his complete inability to understand how it could come about that if a man were, on examination, found to have been entitled to an increase in pay for a year or so anterior to the date of such determination, the increase in pay is justified, whereas a simultaneous determination that the work the man was doing for the same period did not justify the rate of pay which he had been drawing and that the classification determination should not be made coterminous. I hope that the hon. member for York South will regard employment in the public service as the giving of a dollar's worth of value for a dollar of pay, rather than some notion that once you get on the payroll you are set for life; that regardless of performance, of the discharge of your responsibility, you are still entitled to continue to receive pay, and not only that, Mr. Chairman, but entitled to benefit from any increases that have probably been earned by others.

I find this a rather difficult philosophy to accept, Mr, Chairman. I think that most self-respecting public servants like to feel that they are working in a system where the reward or emolument is continuously commensurate with their performance. We have insisted on the merit system, which I think is an excellent one, rather than the system of seniority. We have engaged fairly continuously over the years in working toward the constant examination of classification and reclassification. During the past three years a rather more intense, massive and, if I may suggest this, rather more intelligent reclassification system has been in progress in which an endeavour has been made to introduce a coherent, continuous system throughout the public service so that everybody is treated fairly; so that we do not have instances where people, largely as a consequence of historical error, or habit, or perhaps persistence in initial mistakes, are being rewarded to an unfair degree compared with others discharging perhaps greater responsibilities and doing harder work who receive less pay.
Recognizing, Mr. Chairman, that this reclassification process would result in some people going up and some going down, the government, acting I think as a good employer, agreed that those who, by reason of reclassification, are found to be entitled to more pay receive this sum in the full amount immediately. On the other hand, those who upon re-examination of their duties and functions are found to be entitled to less pay are not required to suffer a decrease in pay but are merely put in a "hold" position and receive no increase in pay until such time as the emolument for the particular office they occupy reaches the level of salary that they are currently enjoying.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I should point out in respect to this red circling that there is a corollary known as green circling. Just as red is considered dangerous and unpleasant, so green is considered pleasant. Of the 82,000 odd positions which were evaluated or re-evaluated in the conversion, about 15,000 were red circled. That is quite a substantial number. As of September 15, 1968, the number of positions that were red circled had been reduced from 15,000 to 1,513. It may perhaps interest hon. members to know that although initially 15,000 persons were red circled, 18,000, coming under a similar general classification, were green circled. In total, more people were green circled, or reclassified upwards, than were red circled or
TMr. Drury.]
reclassified downwards. This system has not led entirely to unhappiness.
I suggested that if as of October 1, the date mentioned by the hon. member for York South, it was determined that a man one year ago was entitled, in respect of his position, to an increase in emolyment it would not be unjust, since he is now doing the same work he did one year ago, to apply the reclassification to him in respect of his upward reassessment for that same period.
The hon. member for Peace River raised two questions, one of which strikes me as interesting. He said that the estimates in some fashion should be portrayed on a five year projection basis so as to enable hon. members to see more clearly the significance of individual items in the estimates. By dealing with items for the previous and current years only, that significance is not so obvious. I think the hon. member's suggestion, if adopted, would make for a much more lucid and descriptive portrayal of government programs. I am not sure what that would do to the blue book of estimates, which already is a massive tome. However I think this project is worthy of examination. Perhaps the most useful way of carrying this out would be in the public accounts committee. Later this evening I hope a proposal will be made that we revert to motions in order to introduce to the public accounts committee a new scheme for setting up estimates which will be vastly more informative, and certainly more descriptive than present arrangements. When the public accounts committee is looking at the program method of portraying estimates, it might also wish to look at the question of doing this on a five year rather than on a one year retroactive and one year prospective basis.
The hon. member for Peace River also said he was unhappy with the system of introducing large supplementary estimates. In his view this was some kind of breach of contract or breach of faith with the public or the house. He may be aware that up until a couple of years ago there was no serious endeavour to include in the estimates all possible and foreseeable items of expenditure during the year. The main estimates might in some cases have been more accurately described as preliminary estimates. In the past two years we have consciously tried to reduce in number and in quantum the size of supplementary estimates. Last year the number of sets of supplementary estimates was limited to three; this year one set of supplementaries has been introduced already, for special reasons, and it is my hope that there will be only
November 18, 1968	COMMONS
one further set of supplementary estimates in the current fiscal year, and that that will be the so-called final sup. If that is done we shall be better able than was the case in previous years to look at entire programs in terms of the main estimates. I think this approach will go a long way to meeting the objections of the hon. member for Peace River.
He also raised the question of loans, investments and advances, indicating that in some instances sums of money represented as loans, investments or advances could more honestly have been portrayed as grants or authorizations to expend in the current year. To a large extent this involves a question of accounting techniques and offers the house the continuing possibility of keeping a finger or a trained eye on the particular amount that is put out by way of loan, investment or advance. Even though the amount is unlikely to be repaid in the foreseeable future, this does mean that the receiving organization, be it a department, agency of government or crown corporation, continues to be accountable until such time as the loan, investment or advance is repaid or discharged. It continues to be accountable for this particular item.
On the other hand, if the amount in question were characterized as a grant or authorization for expenditure, the accountability in respect of the amount presumably would cease during the currency of the fiscal year in question. This is something we might look at and see whether in some instances sums provided by way of loans, investments or advances might more usefully and accurately be classified as grants or authorizations to expend.
I think I have covered most points raised in respect of these estimates, though I might add one observation in respect of some remarks made by the hon. member for York South about red circling and reclassification. I am told that the effective date of reclassification in almost every instance has been discussed with the bargaining units during the negotiating process. To suggest that the action taken by the government has been unilateral-I think he used the term "ukase"-is inaccurate. The retroactivity of the reclassification has been discussed with the bargaining units in most instances during the process of negotiation.

When he was speaking a few minutes ago, the minister seemed to confirm that there was a change of government attitude-that in the earlier part of 1967 there was a favourable disposition to act on this matter, but that in the latter part of the year the government concluded that it was necessary to make certain cuts, that it was obliged to practise a certain amount of financial retrenchment. The minister intimated, if I understood him correctly, that the government had reduced its estimates and was trying to live within the confines of its revised estimates. I would remind him that the revised estimates are of course much larger than they were before they were revised. When these estimates are broken in so many respects, and when the figures are inflated in so many cases, I find it difficult to understand why these people should be called upon to be deprived of the pension increases to which they feel they are entitled, because of the so-called practice of economy. Every time the government announces that cuts are to be made and the budget balanced, the net result is the spending of more money. Yet these people who have a justifiable claim are told they have to wait.
If the minister is going to imply that increasing these pensions is somehow or other taxing the people of Canada, he will have to try to explain this to those pensioners who know there is about $3 billion in the fund, and that it is growing rapidly every year, because the interest alone represents more than is paid out in pensions, not to speak of the new contributions that is paid in.
I do not really profess to understand the mechanics, the financing, the economics of this, but I can follow the reasoning of people on the government side when they explain that this money has no existence except as figures in a book, and so. on. But try to explain that to these people who worked for the government for 20, 30 or 35 years and who paid their money in-or, at least, they did not get it in their pay cheques. Try to explain to them that the money is not there, that it is just figures in a book and that they cannot get it, or a reasonable rate of interest on it, without there being a charge on the people of the country.
I know that all pensions are a charge on current production; I have proclaimed it many times. But the minister had better explain this to these people, and in ways that nobody else has yet been able to do satisfactorily. As they see it, the simple fact of the

matter is that when they were working they were asked to take home, not 100 per cent of their pay but 931 per cent or 95 per cent, whatever the rate was at the time. I hope he will take it back to the cabinet and remind his colleagues that in the early part of 1967 the government of the day was almost persuaded that this was a just cause and that something should be done about it.
