I should like to take two or three minutes, if I may, to comment on that. No doubt the President of the Treasury Board will correct me if I have misunderstood his comments.
First, I was glad to have the minister confirm the fact that there were some thousands-I understand he said 15,000 odd-public service employees who were red circled. I was not questioning the fact that there is value in reclassifying jobs. I was questioning the fact that it was done without consultation with the organization, and as I said earlier I was particularly outraged by the fact that some people did not receive their retroactive pay because the red circling was made retroactive in some cases for a full year. I could see no reason for that. It is neither my suggestion nor that of anyone else who has any knowledge of this thing that the jobs must remain in precisely the same relationship to each other, despite changes in the work load and work content; but I believe it is better labour relations not to make changes which affect thousands of people without consultation with their spokesmen.
If that suggestion appears to the President of the Treasury Board to be one sided, then I should tell him the comments which I understand he made were certainly not two sided; they were certainly the management view that it is entirely within management's power and authority to reclassify and readjust without consultation and without other people knowing what is being done.

I should point out to the hon. gentleman that I did say that the effective dates of reclassification have been the subject
Supply-Treasury Board of discussion during the course of negotiations. This has not been done without consultation or unilaterally or by ukase.

I am glad to have that assurance. All I can say to the President of the Treasury Board is that those who spoke for the employees at the negotiating tables were not under that impression. They were under the impression they were being told what the date was. They were informed of the date on which the red circling would become effective retroactively. If that is what the President of the Treasury Board means by discussion and consultation, then he and I had better look up a dictionary. If they were told the red circling would take effect on a certain day, some of them may not have protested, but in many cases they did. The representatives of the employees should have been asked for their comments. That is what I mean by consultation. I do not mean that he should sit down and tell them what he has decided to do. That is not discussion either. So far as my information is concerned that is all that happened.
I should like to know by what philosophy or social or moral thesis an employer has a right to make red circling retroactive. If I have worked a year in a certain class and you take unto yourself the power to change my class today, I suggest that is enough; but by what right do you take it within your power to tell me that in the past twelve months, even though I worked with the knowledge that I was in a certain class-not merely the impression but the knowledge-putatively, as we lawyers would say, I must be considered to have been in a lower class one year ago? On what basis do you place that kind of an imposition on an employee affected by red circling, and what purpose does it serve except to create bitterness and resentment, which is entirely justified?
This was the major point I drew to the attention of the President of the Treasury Board. I am told that that point was not answered and I should like to know what the answer is. It is bad enough for one to be told that his work is not worth as much as he thought it was in relation to the job-and I do not deny your right to say that. But by what right can you push someone back a whole year in that new lower classification? That is the major point.
The second point in respect of which I understand he said I was being one sided, because all my experience was one sided-it was, and I make no apology-was that concerning the employer having the right to state

November 18, 1968
Supply-Treasury Board his limits and the union having the right to state its demands. Surely the point is that in good labour relations in the government service one must forget that the government is a pretty important and pretty powerful agency.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
In my experience in collective bargaining, and there are others in this chamber who have had experience, I cannot recall any case, in which I was involved, and I have been involved in thousands of them, when the president of a company went on television or on radio and said through that medium to his negotiators at the negotiating table and the public of Canada that he was not going to give more than "X" amount. He might do that after the negotiations have broken down, but I have not known the head of an ordinary private company, who has any sense about labour negotiations, doing that during negotiations. He sends his instructions to his negotiators.
When the employer of the public service, who is the governor and ultimately the public, does that in the course of negotiation- that is, gets on the public platform, along with the President of the Treasury Board-
I didn't.
I beg your pardon; you did not?
It is terribly hard to compete with T.V. personalities today. I outlined all this.

In any event, when the Prime Minister does that I suggest he is doing something which is not good for labour relations in the public service. If those are the instructions they should go to the government's negotiators at the negotiating table. When the Prime Minister makes such a statement to the people of Canada, who ultimately are the taxpayers out of whose money these salaries are paid, what does this do to those people and what does it do to postal and seaway employees vis-a-vis the people of Canada? I do not know whether this occurred at the same time, but the Prime Minister added something about squeezing a lemon, and that there is only so much juice in a lemon. He said he was not going to be a lemon, or something to that effect. What does this do to the negotiators on behalf of the government and the employees, vis-a-vis the public of Canada? If I were one of the employees affected I would make a devil of a lot of noise
if the Prime Minister did that during negotiations which my representatives were attempting to carry out. There is no need for this. There is no need to create public opinion which impinges on postal and seaway employes, putting them under the gun in that way.
The government has negotiators at the negotiating table. It should send them its instructions, and they will pass them on to the negotiating committee of the workers concerned. Surely that is the way to carry on negotiations. No matter what the President of the Treasury Board may say, this is a ukase when it is stated by the Prime Minister with all the power and knowledge the government has in relation to everybody concerned in the bargaining process, particularly during an election campaign. The President of the Treasury Board or his colleagues cannot tell me that is legitimate bargaining, as the law puts it, in good faith. If that is so, then I should like to know what bad faith in bargaining is. I repeat the warning I gave earlier: If this is the road that is to be followed, there is going to be a great deal more trouble in the future than we have had in the past.

Item agreed to.
5. Contingencies-Subject to the approval of the Treasury Board, to supplement other votes for paylist and other requirements and to provide for miscellaneous minor and unforeseen expenses not otherwise provided for including awards under the Public Servants Inventions Act, and authority to re-use any sums allotted for non-paylist requirements and repaid to this appropriation from other appropriations, $70,000,000.

Mr. Chairman, I have one or two things to say about this contingency fund. It is only right that we should ask the President of the Treasury Board a few questions about this blank cheque for $70 million, representing an increase from $45 million, that he is asking us to give. We have a few fond memories about this contingency or slush fund which covers the waterfront and takes in almost everything. We recall one time when we were dealing with interim supply in this house, which was not granted as soon as the government thought it should have been. The government went to work on this fund and found enough money to pay the bills and take this club away from the opposition. We have not forgotten that. The minister should explain the purpose of this fund to the house.
As I suggest, this covers the waterfront. It says, for instance it can be used, subject to

November 18, 1968	COMMONS
the approval of the Treasury Board, to supplement other votes for pay lists. In other words, if there is some increase in pay in different departments this fund will presumably take care of them. It is my thought that if a department estimates its expenditures for salaries and does not estimate them correctly, it should come back to the house and ask for a supplementary amount so that parliament will know the use to which the money is supposed to be put.
The item also suggests that this fund can be used for other requirements and to provide for miscellaneous, minor and unforeseen expenses. That is about as broad as it could be. Why do we not just say that it is to cover everything, instead of trying to dress it up with a whole lot of fancy words? This is as wide and as open as the sky. It refers to unforeseen expenses not otherwise provided for, including awards under the Public Servants Inventions Act. I am not too familiar with that act and I think the minister should tell us what it is all about. The item refers also to an authority to re-use any sums allotted for non-paylists. In other words, this includes anything that has nothing to do with salaries but has been allotted in the estimates, not used and repaid into this contingency fund. As I understand it this refers to all the departments of government, not just the Treasury Board. It refers to any estimates that had been passed in the house other than for salaries, which have not been used. They can be put back into this contingency fund and the Treasury Board has a blank cheque to use this for anything they decide. This is a very important vote and parliament should know what it is passing in respect of this $70 million.

Mr. Chairman, as the hon. gentleman has indicated, the principal amount to be granted in this vote is to cover expected, although undetermined salary increases as a consequence of bargaining negotiations now taking place. The hon. gentleman will realize that we are now in full swing of negotiations. All of these negotiations or agreements have resulted in over-all increases in wages and salaries. In order to avoid indicating in advance of the bargaining process what one might describe as the final offer, which in respect of the government service has not yet been done either publicly or privately, the amount is put into the contingency fund with the understanding that in the final supplementary estimates the amounts required to
DEBATES	2893
Supply-Treasury Board meet the salary increases arising out of collective bargaining agreements, which may have been concluded by then, will be made up in the final supplementary estimates. This accounts for the bulk of the amount.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
As the hon. gentleman has indicated, there are a number of paylist items. I have examples of that kind of thing for the previous year. It is impossible to say what unforeseen contingencies will occur in a current fiscal year. Equally it is a little difficult to say what precisely, and of what value, will be the inventions made by people in the public service during the course of the fiscal year.
Would the minister mind running down that list and giving us, not the amounts of money but the headings under which those amounts were paid out?
Does the hon. member mean the non-pay list?
Yes, Mr. Chairman.

The 1967-68 list runs to quite a few items. June 27, 1967, payments to eligible milk producers, $209; construction of road through Kapuskasing experimental farm, $10,000; payment to owners of crops destroyed by the Golden Nematode, $60,600; funds to the Canadian Dairy Commission for the payment of audit fees, $30,000. Those are some items in the Department of Agriculture. Then under the heading of chief electoral officer we have $2,500 for commissionaire services and travelling expenses. Under the relatively new Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs we have expenses of the task force on Canada Corporations Act, $152,400; expenses of task force on securities, $46,500; federal government's share of committee on mutual funds and investments contracts, $142,525; expenses of consumer affairs branch, $175,000. These are the kind of items that are on this list.
Under the heading of Energy, Mines and Resources there is the item for expenses of Canadian steering committee of international association on water pollution, $5,000; expenses of Crow's Nest industries team to world series of safety competitions, $2,000. Under the heading of External Affairs there is the item, protection of diplomatic property in Canada, $75,000. The hon. gentlemen will recollect that some damage was caused to the premises of the diplomatic mission here, an occurrence which understandably cannot be

November 18, 1968
Supply-Treasury Board foreseen before the year begins. Next we have purchase of Beaver aircraft for assistance to Middle East refugees, $139,000. Then, there is the study of external aid programs, $50,000; Italian earthquake relief, $100,000. Under the Department of Fisheries we have the item for fishing vessel construction subsidies, $300,000. It will be recollected that the rate at which fishermen availed themselves of this offer of a subsidy turned out to be higher than forecast.
Under the heading of the Canadian livestock feed board there is the item for general administration expenses, $30,000. Under the heading of Indian Affairs and Northern Development there is forest fire fighting in Yukon, $130,000, and grant to commissioner of Northwest Territories in establishing new government in Yellowknife, $175,000. Under the Department of Labour there is the item for allowances and expenses of conciliation boards and industrial inquiry commissions, $30,000. Under the heading of the Senate there is the item for the expenses of the Senate committee, $115,000, on two separate occasions. Under the House of Commons, December 14, 1967 there is the item for additional funds for publishing debates, $240,000. Under Manpower and Immigration there is the item of operating grants to the provinces under the former technical and vocational training agreements, $11 million.
I have a few more pages of these items but I think what I read gives an indication of the nature of these non-pay list items.

Mr. Chairman, it certainly gives us an idea of what goes on. I do not think one could call more than a third of these items emergency or contingency items. Many of them should be estimates under the department, such as for instance audit fees in the Department of Agriculture, chief electoral officer, purchase of Beaver aircraft, livestock feed board, new government at Yellowknife, and House of Commons debates. All these are more or less permanent items, could have been foreseen and should have been in the estimates for these various departments. I do not think we can call all of these contingencies. The minister did read out some that were contingencies, and I am sure hon. members would agree to that; but, goodness knows, this account is not being used for what it was set up for.
I hope the day will come when we will have a committee of this house, whether it is the public accounts committee or a part of

the Treasury Board, where members of parliament will agree to these expenditures before they are approved. The way it is now, parliament leaves these decisions in the hands of Treasury Board, and who does Treasury Board consist of but the five ministers on the front benches? The opposition has nothing to say about it, and the money is spent and gone. This house needs a committee where members from all parties would sit down and deal with these contingencies. Believe me, a lot of these contingencies would be wiped out and there would be proper estimating if we had such a committee.

Mr. Chairman, I was a member of the public accounts committee at the time of the pay scandal-that is the only word I can use for it-and it is then I believe that I invented the phrase "slush fund", because that is all this fund was at that time. It amounted to $45 million, and I was assured by the then president of the Treasury Board that this would never occur again, and that it was an accident. The government of that time found the money in the slush fund and thus frustrated parliament. Parliament thought that its members had the traditional right of denying Her Majesty supply, but what in fact happened was that the different departments got together and found $100,000 here and $100,000 there, and if my memory serves me correctly over $2 million was found by accident with which to pay the civil servants of Canada. In this way the opposition was not able to bring forcibly to the attention of the nation the scandalous way in which our finances were being managed. Now we are asked to vote some $70 million, which is very close to double the amount the government had a few years back when this trouble occurred.
Unless I miss my guess, with the $70 million the government will have a great deal more leeway than it had with the $45 million. By carelessly voting $45 million we frustrated ourselves in our right to criticize the government and all its departments. We discussed this very thoroughly in the public accounts committee and we decided to try to plug this hole. We even asked the officials of the departments for their advice on how this sort of thing could be stopped so that it could never occur again. Now I am astounded to see that our recommendation, which were very strong at that time, that no $45 million of unmarked money should be left lying around for such a contingency, has been completely disregarded
November 18, 1968	COMMONS
and that we are asked for some $70 million to be paid into exactly the same kind of fund.
For fear that what I say may sound like nothing but criticism I have a suggestion to make, namely that none of this money be allowed to spill over to allow the government of the day to get out of the hole. If we are in fact putting money in which has already been spent, and this is only a general fund to cover up legitimate expenses in individual departments, such as fire fighting costs and costs for refitting of ships and a setting up of a new government for the Northwest Territories, that is fine and dandy; but we want to be assured here and now that this fund will not again be abused as it was before. Apparently the promises of Treasury Board are not enough, because I suspect that if we approve this $70 million without receiving some assurance from Treasury Board that this fund will not be abused, we will have a repetition of the trouble we had once before, but with nearly twice as much money with which to play around.
I wonder if the minister would assure me that he will do all he can to see that this particular abuse of our trust in the financial administration of this country will not be used as a club over the heads of the opposition, and indeed over parliament itself.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)

It is quite difficult to answer that, Mr. Chairman. I do not believe I can accept the statement that the government has abused the trust of parliament in the use of this particular fund. If I gave that assurance, it would be implied that the trust was used as a club with which to beat parliament on some previous occasion. If it is quite clear there has not been any such previous occasion, I am quite prepared to do all I can to see that this contingency fund is not employed as an abusive trust, nor will it be employed as a club with which to beat parliament.

I think the answer is not too difficult to give. Suppose there are 20 departments that need some type of contingency fund, then I am quite willing to vote them a percentage of, say, 10 per cent of their yearly appropriation for this purpose. However, I am not prepared to see the fund spill over into other departments and used in a way to frustrate parliament when it comes to voting supply. This fund should not be used for paying civil servants or for other departmental purposes. If there is an over-appropriation, then that amount should go back into the con-
DEBATES	2895
Supply-Treasury Board solidated revenue fund or perhaps used as a general contingency fund.
However, the contingency fund should not be used to get the government out of a bind. The government sometimes finds money which we did not know about, which we did not vote for a particular purpose, and they pull it out of a hat, like a magician at a sideshow. Then the government says to parliament, "Ha ha, we have the money; there is no point in continuing the supply debate. We have paid the civil servants"-or the mounted police, as the case may be. In this way the historical right of the opposition to question the government about spending money is frustrated. We are not able to discuss the estimates of every department in parliament. The time allotted to the supply debate runs out and we are probably able to discuss only five departments a year. Perhaps on the last supply vote of the year we are able to refer to certain things which we believe are abuses, and bring them forcibly to the attention of the government by means of a long debate. If this opportunity is going to be taken away by frustrating the opposition's right to grant supply, then I feel parliament is being frustrated. I think it is the duty of Treasury Board and the government as well to put this voluntary check on their own abuses. It is not a question of whether or not there are abuses. Naturally we trust the government to do its best, but they have made mistakes from time to time.
If our system of party government has any value at all, then it lies in the fact that the opposition is able to bring forward what they believe is an abuse. It is not yet treason in Canada to criticize the goverment; it is our duty.

PUBLIC WORKS-MONTMAGNY, QUE.- REQUEST FOR DREDGING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for having taken into consideration the question I asked some time ago with regard to a problem concerning my riding, and more particularly the people of ile-aux-Grues and the town of Montmagny.
Is is about a wharf, the Montmagny Wharf built a number of years ago, thanks to the contribution of both the government and a private enterprise. At that time, the wharf was meeting the needs of the population and was capable of promoting the economic development of the area.
Opposite the city of Montmagny there is an island inhabited by good citizens, 90 per cent of them farmers, especially potato growers and milk producers. The only useful means of communication between Ile-aux-Grues and the city of Montmagny is by boat.
But for some years now, the situation has been worsening. The channel leading to the wharf at Montmagny, which is commonly called the dock channel, is so full of sand and mud that this fall, even at high tide, the ship that plies between Ile-aux-Grues, the big island and the city of Montmagny had a hard time docking, often damaging its engine. In fact, the owner, Mr. Lavoie, is wondering if he will be able much longer to
November 18, 1968

carry the produce, the mail and the people who have to keep in touch with the rest of the province and the country. In short, the people have the right to live on that island and they are also entitled to the services which are normal in 1968 with regard to communications, health, etc.
The government authorities in Ottawa have been aware of that problem for a number of years now because, during the week, a special meeting took place between the city council of Montmagny and the intermediate bodies. Of course, I was invited to take part in that study in order to submit the problem once again to Ottawa and to try to convince the authorities of the urgency of doing something.
Studies were made two, three or four years ago, and estimates were prepared by engineers. According to present day flies, it seems that it would cost approximately half a million dollars to dredge the channel and give the ships access to the wharf, thus facilitating navigation and communications.
I feel that, even though it should not be extremely profitable or advantageous for the government, something should be done to help that area of the province of Quebec, if not to develop further at least to maintain itself economically.
Mr. Speaker, it is common knowledge that the lower St. Lawrence, from Montmagny down, has numerous economic difficulties. All the governments, co-operate in trying to maintain an interesting and decent standard of living, as well as agricultural and industrial organizations with a view to encouraging the people to stay in that beautiful part of our country. I insist on this and I shall continue to insist, because it is my duty. It is not an election commitment because, before the elections, a questionnaire had been submitted to me in order to know my ideas on the subject and I deliberately omitted to reply, in order not to give the impression that I promised to solve problems which I did not understand.
I did not want to enter into any commitment, but today I am their spokesman in the house and since I understand their problems better, it is my duty to try to work with the government in order to find solutions which will be beneficial, valuable and lasting.
There is another aspect to the problem which must be remembered, and that is that a great many migratory birds come to l'ile-aux-Grues in the autumn. The hunting season attracts many tourists to the island and is an important source of revenue for the people. However, because navigation is difficult, there
2897
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion are fewer hunters each year, and therefore less profit to be made. In my opinion, taking into consideration all those problems concerning l'ile-aux-Grues and the town of Montmagny, it would be in the national interest to take the steps necessary to solve them as soon as possible, so that the people do not feel neglected. They should be given the same help as is given elsewhere. This is not always economically sound but it is necessary from the humanitarian point of vue.

That was the report of the special joint committee on the Public Service of Canada and it was the report that recommended increases in the pensions of retired civil servants.
The Minister of Finance indicated that, in his view, there were technical difficulties in concurring in the report of a committee made to a previous parliament. As a result of that I endeavoured to help the government by proposing the next day, on Friday, November 8, a motion to take that report into review during the present session. I presented that motion on Friday, November 8, as reported in Hansard at page 2567. There was not the necessary unanimous consent, so the motion was not allowed. In stating his objection the President of the Privy Council said that there
28g8	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion would be opportunities during the current session to deal with that report.
When I posted this matter for one of these adjournment debates I did not realize it would come at the end of a day on which we have had a fair amount of discussion on the whole question of pensions of retired civil servants. Although we did not reach any conclusion that might be called satisfactory during our discussions today I was happy that the President of the Treasury Board agreed that the matter could and should be discussed again by the cabinet.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Perhaps I should leave it there instead of pressing my questions of November 7 and 8. Perhaps I should simply ask the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gray) if he will confirm the statement that the matter will be discussed in cabinet. I know he is not in the cabinet, but I also know he is close to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and if he will just let the Minister of Finance know that this commitment has been made by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) and express the hope that consideration will be given at an early date, that will be a measure of progress.

I do not think a lengthy debate would be necessary and I believe a vote for it would be unanimous. My hope is that if we can take this step we can get back to the mood that I think the government was in between January and June of 1967 and get action on this matter at an early date.

I hope he will give us the best answer he can, and that at least he will give us an assurance that he will endeavour to see that his minister takes part in the discussion of this matter in cabinet, and also that he will do his best to get an opportunity for the house to express its view, which I am sure will be unanimous, that the time has come to provide these increases in the pensions of our federal superannuates, without any further delay.

RURAL DEVELOPMENT-PROPOSED CENTRALIZATION OF ATLANTIC REGION PEOPLE
speechtext:
Some time ago, on November 7 to be precise,
I asked the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development (Mr. Marchand) to give us some indication whether the government was actively studying the sociological and economic circumstances surrounding the centralization of the people of the Atlantic region.
My question arose out of the statement of the minister in Halifax to the effect that we must look to regional interests but we must not confuse this with being parochial; regional development did not mean there would be more jobs in every county, a new plant at every crossroad or a new wharf in every harbour. The minister went on to indicate that the countryside is losing people and that many villages and small towns are declining in population. He went on further to infer that people would be expected to migrate. The whole inference of this was that the department had made plans for the centralization of the people of the Atlantic region.
A few days earlier, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) referred to the fact that some 8,000 people would be centralized under a resettlement plan in Newfoundland. That is, 15 per cent of the people of Newfoundland would be brought from small rural communities to urban communities within the next ten years. As a matter of fact on Friday, November 15, one of our local newspapers in a commentary indicated that centralization is probably the biggest single issue the province has had to grapple with at any time in modern history. It said it can mean the future progress and stability of the province or its economic and social ruin. That editorial was entitled, "Don't Play With People."
An eminent Canadian author has characterized the decentralization carried on by the federal and provincial governments as the concentration of people into concentration camps before they move to Toronto.
The reason I pose my question to the minister, and would like a statement from
November 18, 1968

him concerning the government's philosophy on resettlement and centralization, is that in actual fact I think the government has no philosophy. Perhaps I should direct my question to the premier of Newfoundland.
This is an important matter of urbanization, centralization, relocation and resettlement, particularly of the people in Newfoundland and of people in the Atlantic region generally. I am not one bit against centralization. I am not against any changes designed by any government, municipal, federal or provincial, to improve the lot of people, provided those changes follow some kind of philosophy, some kind of plan, some kind of program, and provided the alternatives have been investigated. My contention is that 8,000 people have been moved, and 80,000 more people are to be moved in Newfoundland without this program being based on any philosophy, plan or policy. I could quote at length from a report investigating the urbanization or relocation of people in Newfoundland, a report commissioned by the federal government.
At page 15 of the report it is pointed out that it would seem the government adopts a policy of hands off, refusing to offer advice to those being moved lest it be held responsible for any unforeseen difficulties that might arise. It does not inquire into the reasons why people should move. The report goes into detail and indicates that people have been moved from slow growth centres to no growth centres. It indicates that housing has been a major problem for people with large families. It indicates that unemployment has resulted. It indicates that elderly people have been forced to relocate in areas where they are virtually faced with starvation.
The report contends that the government has been dealing with the benefits accruing to young people from the program, with no regard given to the problems faced by the adult segment of the population resulting from relocation. The government has a narrow concept of centralization. It intimates that the government has literally been playing checkers with people, expecting people to leave a sinking ship and jump into the raging Atlantic.
It is heartbreaking to study many of the problems faced by people who have been relocated in Newfoundland. As a result of relocation now we have the man without a home as compared to the man with a home, the man Edward Markham and Millais painted and wrote about.
I am asking the government for a statement of its philosophy. I am asking it to take a
2899
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion closer look at what it is doing with people, because centralization is not the sole solution for many of the problems of rural Atlantic Canada. I am asking the government to inform the people of the Atlantic region, in fact of all regions in Canada whether west or east, what its policies are in this matter.
We have had instances where people have been moved to a new location and found they could not afford to buy houses. People get $1,000 to move and $200 per child, and sometimes they are moved into areas where the cost of living for them has increased fivefold. When the government moves people I ask it to consider the humanist aspects involved and not just the economic aspects.
I think the minister in charge of rural development has a clear concept of what is involved. I am convinced of this from reading his statements in the maritimes. All I am asking is that the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis), who now has responsibility for the program, and the minister in charge of regional development, get their heads together along, with provincial officials, and indicate to the people of Canada what their philosophy is. Right now there seems to be no philosophy, and what does appear is tragedy for a good number of people in many regions of Canada.

speechtext: November 18, 1968

1.	The North Atlantic Council met in ministerial session in Brussels on 15th and 16th November. The meeting was attended by foreign, defence and finance ministers. The [DOT]council had moved forward from mid-December its normal year-end meeting so that ministers might discuss at an earlier date the serious situation following the armed intervention in Czechoslovakia and the occupation of that country by forces of the Soviet union *and of four of its Warsaw pact allies.
2.	Ministers reaffirmed the inviolability of the principle, which has been invoked on numerous occasions by every country, including the USSR, that all nations are independent and that consequently any intervention by one state in the affairs of another is unlawful.
They noted that this principle has been deliberately violated by the Soviet leaders with the backing of four of their allies. World opinion has been profoundly shocked by this armed intervention carried out against the wishes of the government and people of Czechoslovakia. All the members of the alliance have denounced this use of force which jeopardises peace and international order and strikes at the principles of the United Nations charter. Like all other peoples, the people of Czechoslovakia must be free to shape their future without outside interference. Agreements concluded under the pressure of occupying forces can provide no justification for challenging this basic concept.
3.	The contention of the Soviet leadership that there exists a right of intervention in the affairs of other states deemed to be within a so-called "Socialist commonwealth" runs counter to the basic principles of the United Nations charter, is dangerous to European security and has inevitably aroused grave anxieties. It gives rise to fears of a further use of force in other cases.
The use of force and the stationing in Czechoslovakia of Soviet forces not hitherto deployed there have aroused grave uncertainty about the situation and about the calculations and intentions of the USSR. This uncertainty demands great vigilance on the part of the allies.
4.	Applied to Germany the policies which the USSR derives from its doctrine of a so-called "Socialist commonwealth" raise new
obstacles to the rapprochement and ultimate unification of the two parts of Germany. Moreover, they would be contrary to the letter and spirit of the four power agreements relating to Germany as a whole.
In this situation, and bearing in mind the special responsibilities of the United States, the United Kingdom and France, the ministers reaffirm the determination of the alliance to persevere in its efforts to contribute to a peaceful solution of the Germany question based on the free decision of the German people and on the interests of European security. Their governments do not recognize the "GDR", and they reject all claims which would tend to perpetuate the division of Germany against the will of the German people.
Referring to their communique issued in Reykjavik on 25th June, 1968, the ministers confirm the support of their governments for the declared determination of the three powers to safeguard Berlin's security and to maintain freedom of access to the city. They recall the declaration of the North Atlantic Council of December 16, 1958 on Berlin and the responsibilities which each member state assumed with regard to the security and welfare of Berlin. They note with satisfaction the important measures taken by the Federal Republic of Germany in conformity with the status of Berlin for the purpose of maintaining the viability of the city. They associate themselves with the position of the three powers as regard the legitimate concern of the federal government for the welfare and viability of Berlin and as regards the resulting ties which exist between the two on the basis of the arrangements in force.
The ministers associate themselves with the call made upon the Soviet union by the three powers to respect the quadripartite agreements concerning Berlin and the decisions taken pursuant to these agreements by the United States, France and the United Kingdom.
5.	The new uncertainties resulting from recent Soviet actions also extend to the Mediterranean basin. This situation requires that the allies continue by every available means their efforts to promote stability and a just and equitable peace, as well as mutual cooperation and understanding, in the area. The
November 18, 1968

expansion of Soviet activity in the Mediterranean, including the increased presence of Soviet naval units, requires vigilance to safeguard allied security.
6.	The members of the alliance urge the Soviet union, in the interests of world peace, to refrain from using force and interfering in the affairs of other states.
Determined to safeguard the freedom and independence of their countries, they could not remain indifferent to any development which endangers their security.
Clearly any Soviet intervention directly or indirectly affecting the situation in Europe or in the Mediterranean would create an international crisis with grave consequences.
7.	So long as the Soviet leaders adhere to a policy of force, these new uncertainties will remain. The allies are convinced that their political solidarity remains indispensable to discourage aggression and other forms of oppression. Above all, they stand wholly determined to meet their common reponsibili-ties and, in accordance with the North Atlantic Treaty, to defend the members of the alliance against any armed attack.
8.	The allies participating in NATO's integrated defence programme have, therefore, been obliged to reassess the state of their defences. They consider that the situation arising from recent events calls for a collective response. The quality, effectiveness, and deployment of NATO's forces will be improved in terms of both manpower and equipment in order to provide a better capability for defence as far forward as possible. The quality to reserve forces will also be improved and their ability to mobilise rapidly will be increased. Renewed attention will be directed to the provision of reinforcements for the flanks and the strengthening of local forces there. The conventional capability of NATO's tactical air forces will be increased. Certain additional national units will be committed to the major NATO commanders. Specific measures have been approved within these categories of action for improving the conventional capability of NATO's forces. Ministers agreed that the co-ordinated implementation of these measures and the provision of additional budgetary resources to the extent necessary to support them would form part of the NATO force plan for 19691973 which will be submitted in January 1969. They also acknowledged that the solidarity of the alliance can be strengthened by co-operation between members to alleviate burdens arising from balance of payments deficits
resulting specifically from military expenditures for the collective defence.
9.	A year ago ministers affirmed in the report on the future tasks of the alliance that, while maintaining adequate military strength and political solidarity to deter any aggressor, the alliance should work to promote a policy of detente. The Soviet intervention in Czechoslovakia has seriously set back hopes of settling the outstanding problems which still divide the European continent and Germany and of establishing peace and security in Europe, and threatens certain of the results already achieved in the field of detente. Indeed, in view of the action of the five members of the Warsaw pact, the scope and level of allied contacts with them have had to be reduced.
10.	More specifically, prospects for mutual balanced force reductions have suffered a severe set back. Nevertheless, the allies in close consultation are continuing their studies and preparations for a time when the atmosphere for fruitful discussions is more favourable.
11.	In any event, consistent with western values the political goal remains that of secure, peaceful and mutually beneficial relations between east and west. The allies are determined to pursue this goal, bearing in mind that the pursuit of detente must not be allowed to split the alliance. The search for peace requires progress, consistent with western security, in the vital fields of disarmament and arms control and continuing efforts to resolve the fundamental issues which divide east and west.
12.	The North Atlantic Alliance will continue to stand as the indispensable guarantor of security and the essential foundation for the pursuit of European reconciliation. By its constitution the alliance is of indefinite duration. Recent events have further demonstrated that its continued existence is more than ever necessary. The foreign minister of France recalled that, for its part, unless events in the years to come were to bring about a radical change in east-west relations, the French government considers that the alliance must continue as long as it appears to be necessary.
13.	The next ministerial meeting of the council will be held in Washington on 10th and 11th April, 1969.
14.	The defence planning committee which met in ministerial session on 14th November will hold its next ministerial meeting in Brussels on 16th January, 1969.
Tuesday, November 19, 1968
